articles.title: UK minister warns of impact of Trump’s Iran war on next month’s budget
articles.summary:
Bridget Phillipson says Burnham’s past criticisms of US president not an issue as PM prepares to meet Trump at UN

Next month’s budget will be made more difficult by Donald Trump’s war with…

blocks.text: Next month’s budget will be made more difficult by Donald Trump’s war with Iran, one of Andy Burnham’s cabinet ministers has said, while adding she did not expect the prime minister’s previous disparaging comments about the US president to be an issue.
Burnham is expected to meet Trump early next week at the UN general assembly summit in New York, the pair having previously spoken twice by phone since Burnham entered No 10.
As Greater Manchester mayor, Burnham said Trump would not be welcome in the city, saying also that UK politicians who indulged him “should be ashamed”.

Asked about the comments, Bridget Phillipson, the Labour chair and minister for women and equalities, told Sky News: “Look, I think what you’ve just described there is politics. The president knows that. This is far from unique.
“People will express views at different points on different topics. And that’s no bar to having a strong relationship.”

She nonetheless repeated UK condemnation of Trump’s on-and-off military campaign against Iran, which has disrupted global oil supplies, causing significant inflationary pressures, saying this would make life more difficult for John Healey, the chancellor, as he plans the budget.
The economy was, Phillipson said, “in a strong position”, especially with growth figures.

She said: “But that’s not to take away from the very real challenges that you identify, particularly where it’s come to the conflict we’ve seen in the Middle East and the impact that that’s been having on businesses and on families close to home.

“We took the decision not to involve ourselves in that conflict. That was the right call. The US will take their own foreign policy decisions, but I believe, and still believe now, it was the right decision for us as a country not to get involved in that conflict. Of course, something that, had Kemi Badenoch and Nigel Farage been running the country, we would have jumped headlong into a conflict with it without end.

“And yet, and we do see the consequences here at home and as we go into the budget, making sure that we are doing everything we can to give people that breathing space to tackle those challenges around the cost of living has been at the forefront of everything that Andy Burnham has done since becoming prime minister.
“I know it’s at the forefront of the chancellor’s mind as he’s planning for that budget later on next month.”
after newsletter promotion

In a later interview with the BBC, Phillipson was dismissive of comments by Jim Ratcliffe, the petrochemicals billionaire, who said this week he had lost confidence in the UK due to levels of immigration and taxation.
She said: “You’ll forgive me if I do take with a pinch of salt what someone who is a tax exile has to say about our country.” Ratcliffe is resident for tax in Monaco.

Burnham has previously defended his comments about Trump in a similar way, saying of the US president: “Well, he’s said things as well, and everyone says things as politicians. In the moment, you meet people where they’re at, and you find a connection with people, and that’s always been my style.”
With the wider UK-US relationship, there were “differences of opinion”, Phillipson said, while arguing that Burnham could see beyond those differences with Trump in maintaining invaluable ties.
She said: “We don’t have the same political outlook, but the relationship between the UK and the US goes beyond any one president, any one prime minister.

“It’s something that has stood the test of time over many centuries, despite political differences. They come and go. What matters most is the British national interest. And that’s what Andy Burnham will deliver for our country.”

articles.title: Sister of Pakistan's ex-PM Imran Khan arrested
articles.summary: Aleema Khanum is accused of mobilising her brother’s supporters ahead of country-wide protests.

blocks.text: The sister of Pakistan's imprisoned former prime minister, Imran Khan, has been arrested ahead of next week's protests held in his support, his Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party has said.
Aleema Khanum was detained in the eastern city of Lahore on Sunday afternoon, PTI officials said, calling it an "illegal detention". Her son is demanding her return.

The order for Khanum's arrest, which came from Lahore's deputy commissioner, alleged that she was mobilising Imran Khan's supporters "through social media and public meetings". It added that she will be detained for 30 days.
Khanum is a vocal critic of her brother's detention, regularly speaking to his supporters and the media.
A police official confirmed Khanum's arrest to the BBC. According to the order, she will be taken to Kot Lakhpat jail in Lahore.
Earlier in the day, her family said they had had "no contact or news of her whereabouts".
"We demand the government immediately disclose her whereabouts and ensure her safe return," Khanum's son Shahrez Khan wrote on X.
Many have linked her arrest to the protests that have been organised across the country on 27 September, when demonstrators plan to march to the Pakistani capital, Islamabad.
The arrest order said Khanum had been mobilising people to "create law and order situations" and "raising/chanting objectionable slogans amongst the general public against the Government."
Streets in Islamabad are already lined with shipping containers, ready to safeguard the city's government buildings.
Local media has reported Pakistan's interior minister as saying that the protests harm the country and that the government will do everything they can to stop them.
Khan has been detained since 2023, when he was sentenced to three years in prison for not declaring money earned from selling gifts he had received while in office.
He has faced charges in over 100 cases, ranging from leaking state secrets to selling state gifts - all of which he has decried as politically motivated.
Last year, the cricket star-turned-politician was jailed for 14 years in a land corruption case - the longest sentence he has received.
While in prison, his health has being deteriorating, and last month Khan had to visit a hospital for an examination.

articles.title: Deaths of three women in sea at Brighton had no criminal involvement, police say
articles.summary:
Jane Adetoro, Christina Walters and Rebecca Walters from Uxbridge were found on 13 May

The deaths of three sisters found in the sea off Brighton beach did not involve any criminality or…

blocks.text: The deaths of three sisters found in the sea off Brighton beach did not involve any criminality or third-party involvement, police have concluded.

The bodies of Jane Adetoro, 36, Christina Walters, 32, and Rebecca Walters, 31, from Uxbridge, west London, were found on 13 May. A postmortem conducted that month confirmed all three women died by drowning.
Specialist detectives worked to trace the sisters’ final movements and understand how they came to be in the water that morning, Sussex police said.
The investigation found all three women were dropped off by taxi at Madeira Drive, the road running along Brighton Beach, at 10.20pm on 12 May, wearing everyday clothing.

No evidence was found to suggest they visited any nightclubs or local businesses in the area at the time and the investigation concluded all three women entered the water near to where their bodies were found, the police spokesperson added.

A spokesperson for the force said: “The purpose of the police investigation was to identify any evidence of criminal offending linked to how the sisters came to be in the water or their subsequent deaths.
“We can confirm the thorough police investigation has not found any evidence of a crime being committed or involvement by a third party.”
Additional details such as the sisters’ specific movements before their deaths and their potential reasons for entering the water will be considered during the East Sussex coroner’s inquest.

Ch Supt Adam Hays said his force had been “acutely aware of the speculation surrounding this incident” and “concerns raised by black communities surrounding the deaths of black people in or near bodies of water”.

He said: “Jane, Rebecca and Christina’s tragic deaths sparked a national outpouring of grief, and I would like to thank everyone who supported our investigation by coming forward with information. We will now support the coronial process and ask that the sisters’ family continue to be given privacy to come to terms with their loss.”

After the sisters’ deaths, their father, Joseph Jacobson, said there were days when the grief felt unbearable but that he held on to the memories they had shared and “the bond that death can never take away”.

In a statement released through Sussex police, Jacobson said: “Jane, Christina and Becky were more than daughters to me: they were my joy, my strength and the beautiful light that filled our family with happiness and love.

“Each of you was unique and precious in your own special way. Your smiles brightened dark days, your laughter brought comfort and your presence made life more meaningful. Though your time on Earth was short, the impact you made will remain in our hearts for ever.”
A GoFundMe online fundraiser for the women’s funerals has received more than 2,200 donations from members of the public, totalling nearly £46,000.

articles.title: Middle East braces for more violence as Iran claims US is planning to renew bombing campaign
articles.summary:
Tensions grow as Trump tells Fox News he is considering ‘wiping Iran out’ after attacks on Riyadh by Houthi rebels

Governments across the Middle East are bracing for an escalation of…

blocks.text: Governments across the Middle East are bracing for an escalation of violence after Iran claimed it had received intelligence that the US was preparing for a renewed bombing campaign against the Islamic Republic.

In a potential sign of growing tensions before the UN general assembly in New York this week, Donald Trump cut short a weekend visit to the Camp David presidential retreat on Sunday with no official explanation, and a new security alert was issued by the state department to all US citizens in the Middle East.

Keeping his options open, Trump reportedly told a Fox News reporter “very big things are going to be happening in the not-so-distant future” and that the options he was considering were “wiping Iran out, letting them rot economically or making a deal”.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps warned that if an attack does take place, “all US bases and interests in the region will become targets of continuous, effective and painful attacks without any limitations or considerations”.

Iran’s leaders also pledged some of the reprisals could extend as far as US naval forces in the Indian Ocean, and accused some Gulf leaders of “double dealing” by allegedly giving a green light to the US attacks.

The outburst of sabre rattling appears to have been prompted by attacks on the Saudi capital Riyadh by Yemen’s Iranian-backed Houthi rebels. The barrage on Saturday marked the first time the capital’s Aramco oil facilities had been subject to such a sustained attck since the Saudi Houthi ceasefire broke down in June. Riyadh insisted it had intercepted the missiles, but local photographs show smoke pouring from the Aramco facility. The port of Yanbu, vital for Saudi oil exports, was also targeted.
The US largely regards the Houthis as a proxy Iranian force and argues that the group’s attacks on Riyadh would not happen without Tehran’s approval, a claim Iran denies.

Trump last week provoked profound questions about the level of US commitment to its Middle East allies when he spurned a call by the Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman asking the US to come to Saudi’s direct military help.

The Saudis wanted US aid after the Houthis suddenly captured strategic ports along Yemen’s west coast overlooking the Red Sea, giving the Houthis control of the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrow waterway that takes commercial shipping through the Red Sea towards Asia.

On the other side of the Arabian peninsular, the strait of Hormuz between Iran and Oman is already effectively closed to western traffic and the pressure on European energy supplies is growing by the day, leading states such as France to take emergency measures to prevent fuel shortages.

In a bid to keep the US out of its war with Saudi Arabia, the Houthis had given commitments to US officials that it would only target Saudi-related shipping in the Red Sea, an undertaking that Trump appeared to regard as sufficient to ensure essential US interests would be protected and that the US need not become involved militarily.

Pressure on the Pentagon budget and dwindling munitions supplies due to the Iran conflict have also made the US reluctant to broaden the theatre of war. Successive bombing campaigns have not dislodged the Houthis, whose lighting advance to the Red Sea coast took the Saudi-backed Yemeni forces by surprise.
Trump appeared to disregard the wider security threat by telling Fox News “The US is in constant contact with the Houthis and they have agreed not to go to war with the US.”
The Houthi government said 318 ships passed through the strait from 10-18 September.

Trump is due to meet the six member states of the Gulf Cooperation Council when he attends the UN general assembly in New York, in a meeting that is likely to cover Iran, Yemen, Gaza and the future of the US security guarantee.

Trump said he was also open to a meeting with Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, in New York, an encounter that would probably be rejected by the Iranians, who refuse to negotiate directly with the US, operating instead largely through mediators. Pezeshkian is one of many world leaders due to address a general assembly that is likely to be dominated, on the sidelines at least, by Trump’s Middle East crisis.

In the first sign of a potential change of White House thinking about renewing US military action, the state department issued a security alert on Saturday to US citizens across the region warning “the security environment remains complex with potential for unforeseen escalation. American citizens in the Middle East should exercise heightened vigilance.”
Hizam al-Assad, a member of the Houthi political bureau, said the attacks on Riyadh are a response to “hundreds of airstrikes that Riyadh had carried out against the people of Yemen”.

In a lengthy statement to parliament on Sunday, Mohammad Ghalibaf, Iran’s chief negotiator, insisted that Iran was not interested in waging a forever war with the US. But the new secretary of the supreme national security council, Mohsen Rezaei, a hardliner, told Al Jazeera that Iran’s seven preconditions for peace – which include the US lifting its blockade of Iran oil ports, the restoration of its frozen assets and the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil exports – remained.

Rezaei also expressed his anger with the Gulf states, saying they had been invited to a meeting in Salahah in Oman last week to approve the agreed Oman-Iran plan for a new authorised shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz, but Saudi Arabia rejected attendance. He said: “We invited them to the Salahah meeting and they reciprocated with a secret meeting in Germany with US Central Command and Israel.”

Despite the Houthi victories last week, forces allied to the UN-recognised government of Yemen claimed to be pushing back against the Houthis across the country with 75 Houthi soldiers killed on Saturday alone.

articles.title: Andy Burnham faces a weakened Trump – but the president remains unpredictable
articles.summary:
The PM hopes to be firmer with the US leader than his predecessor without provoking diplomatic warfare, as the Iran war weighs on the UK economy

No international relationship has more power…

blocks.text: No international relationship has more power to determine the success of Andy Burnham’s premiership. So you might imagine the stakes for the prime minister’s first face-to-face meeting with Donald Trump on Tuesday would be high.

Yet Burnham may prove to be a lucky general. The balance of risk has shifted. Trump is unpopular at home, where inflation remains high, and is mired in an intractable conflict in Iran that has the potential to sink his midterm dreams.

When Keir Starmer first visited Trump in February 2025, the situation could not have been more different. The notoriously unpredictable president had just won the US election and was at the height of his powers – and was showing muscle on Nato and Ukraine, and with threats of tariffs.

Starmer’s “keep calm and carry on” strategy helped keep Trump on board the defence alliance and also protected the UK from the worst of his aggression over trade. But it came with a cost: he was often left looking obsequious and at odds with the national mood.

Burnham defended his predecessor’s approach but in June signalled he would take a different direction. “Obviously the relationship is important to the UK, but not to the point where we just go along with anything they say,” he said. “We’ve got in trouble in the past when that happens.”

Downing Street insiders expect Burnham to be a bit more forceful when he feels there’s a need to stand up for British interests. But there is no suggestion he will follow the more combative approach of Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister.

Instead, one source said he would probably take a “third way” between Starmer and Carney, pushing back more than his predecessor publicly and privately, but avoiding open diplomatic warfare. A second source said the prime minister had three ambitions for Tuesday’s talks: bond with Trump, make the case for Ukraine, and avoid any drama.

Early clues about how the talks might go from the White House perspective have been mixed. In June, Trump suggested Burnham was “extremely liberal” (not as a compliment) and dismissively described him as the “mayor of a town”.

The US president remains angry the UK did not join his strikes on Iran, and has attacked the country as a “dying” nation “on the edge of disaster”. More recent comments that he might not help if Argentina again tried to seize the Falklands, and that he would love to see a united Ireland, suggest his displeasure has not abated.

But that will not necessarily translate into a strained personal relationship with Burnham. The pair have spoken on the phone twice and are said to have got on. The prime minister’s laid-back, confident style is likely to go down well with Trump, who has already shown with the New York mayor, Zohran Mamdani, that he can warm to leftwingers.

On policy too, government insiders point to small reasons for hope: Trump responded warmly to reports the UK government was going to “open up” the North Sea (although the decision to drill at two fields has been delayed) and has – so far – been relatively restrained when asked about the UK’s planned West Bank settlement trade ban.
Their meeting will be fraught with tension over both matters, and other areas – such as defence spending and the Iran war – have potential for further clashes.

It will help Burnham that Tuesday’s talks will be held on the comparatively neutral ground of the UN, rather than at the White House. As such, he will avoid the jeopardy of an Oval Office press conference that Trump could easily derail.

Trump may also decide he has had enough fights for one day. His meeting with Burnham will follow his address to the UN. Last year Trump told world leaders their countries were “going to hell” over their immigration policies. The UK meeting may end up as just a sideshow.
after newsletter promotion

Burnham’s views on Trump have also shifted since he took office. As mayor of Greater Manchester, he said the US president would not be welcome in the city, blaming his “poisonous” politics. After winning his seat as an MP in Makerfield, he warned against the “divided, dark politics” of the US.

But over the summer, Burnham appeared to shrug off potential divisions, telling reporters that “everyone says things as politicians”. The new prime minister said he would “say what I feel” to Trump but – crucially – would also try to “find a connection” with the mercurial president.

With Trump now weaker domestically, political power in the US is starting to shift to who comes next. Burnham is walking into the room with a president who is running out of time. Yet Trump is in power for two more years, and he is nothing if not unpredictable.

Burnham’s priority may be on domestic affairs, but his closest aides acknowledge that the biggest weight on the UK right now is Trump’s war in Iran. While the war continues to wreak damage on the British economy, Burnham will struggle to deliver his promises of change.
So for the time being, the power still rests with Trump, and Burnham may yet find he has to navigate a perilous path as Starmer did before him.

articles.title: 18 suspects in 2021 assassination of Haiti leader to be extradited to U.S. to face trial
articles.summary: Eighteen suspects who were arrested in the July 2021 killing of Haitian President Jovenel Moïse were awaiting extradition to the U.S. on Sunday, marking the end of a drawn-out judicial process in…

image.caption: A police officer holds up handcuffs in a Port-au-Prince court on June 2 that were allegedly carried by suspects accused of being involved in the assassination Haitian President Jovenel Moïse. (Odelyn Joseph/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

Eighteen suspects who were arrested in the July 2021 killing of Haitian President Jovenel Moïse were awaiting extradition to the U.S. on Sunday, marking the end of a drawn-out judicial process in Haiti for a killing that shocked the troubled Caribbean country.
Officials say dozens have been indicted, arrested in killing of Jovenel Moïse
The suspects will face trial in Florida, according to U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Florida Jason Reding Quiñones.

"Today marks the next major phase in our pursuit of accountability for the assassination of President Jovenel Moïse," he wrote on X. "We will follow the evidence wherever it leads, to those who financed it, facilitated it, supported it or committed crimes to make it possible. Five years later, we are still bringing defendants before American courts, and we are not finished."
Quiñones did not identify the suspects, but those who remain in Haiti awaiting trial include more than a dozen Colombian soldiers and a former Haitian government official.
Quiñones said 30 people have been indicted in Moïse's killing, with FBI Special Agent in Charge Brett Skiles noting that there were multiple arrests in the U.S. and abroad on Sunday.
He said that the FBI and others "remain steadfast in ensuring that all individuals who allegedly sought profit from the assassination of a head of state are held fully accountable."
The extradition comes as the U.S. continues to prosecute and sentence multiple other suspects in the case.
In May, a jury in Florida convicted four men in the killing, and at least five others have pleaded guilty and are serving life sentences.

Those recently convicted include Arcangel Pretel Ortiz, Antonio Intriago, Walter Veintemilla and James Solages, all of whom pleaded not guilty. A jury found them guilty of conspiring to kill or kidnap Haiti's elected leader and providing material support for the plot.

articles.title: Friedrich Merz vows to stay in office after CDU ‘disaster’ in German state elections
articles.summary:
Far-right AfD wins in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and leftwing Die Linke on course for victory in Berlin

Germany’s embattled chancellor, Friedrich Merz, has vowed to stay in office and…

blocks.text: Germany’s embattled chancellor, Friedrich Merz, has vowed to stay in office and fight for future-proofing economic changes despite heavy losses for his conservatives in two state elections, one to the far right and the other to a leftwing party.

Preliminary results indicated Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU) tallied just over the 5% threshold to enter the state parliament in the coastal region of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, its worst-ever state score, which he called a “disaster”.

The anti-immigration, Kremlin-friendly Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party extended a streak of strong showings by coming in first in the former communist region with nearly 38%, more than doubling its previous score.

In the capital, Berlin, one of Germany’s 16 federal states, the far-left Die Linke looked on course to win with about 25% of the vote, ahead of the incumbent CDU by a five-point margin. The AfD made headway there too, with a clear double-digit result.
The deeply unpopular Merz has been fighting for his political survival after a humiliating series of setbacks with voters this year.
Speculation about his ability to hold on as chancellor reached fever pitch after Saxony-Anhalt state’s AfD chapter routed the CDU with a record 44% for the party in an election two weeks ago.

The Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania result marked the third time the AfD has emerged as the strongest party in a region, although the party seemed likely to remain shut out of power in the state because of a “firewall” of non-cooperation agreed by the other main parties.

In a rare speech on a state election night, Merz admitted the CDU had been bitterly deprived of “tailwinds from Berlin” in both of Sunday’s races. But he said he would remain chancellor and party chair and continue a reform drive on fronts including taxes, healthcare, pensions and reducing bureaucracy.
Merz said the German economy was facing “profound upheaval”, while public discourse had become “harsher and more irreconcilable”.
“Trust in our country’s institutions is waning and is being actively undermined by radical parties on both the left and the right,” he said.

But he added: “Germany is capable of reform. I would even go so far as to say that these reforms are the antidote to the poison of authoritarianism, which is penetrating ever deeper into our society as the fascination with authoritarianism grows.”

blocks.caption: The AfD’s co-chair, Tino Chrupalla, react as he hears the first results of the Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania state election in Schwerin. Photograph: Lisi Niesner/Reuters

blocks.text: A jubilant AfD co-leader, Tino Chrupalla, mocked Merz before his speech, saying voters had given his own party a “very clear result” and called on the chancellor to resign.
About 2.5 million people were eligible to vote in Berlin and nearly 1.3 million in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

The stinging blows from the latest elections had been expected to put pressure on Merz at a minimum to cede the CDU leadership, which would have in effect ruled out a run for re-election at the next national poll, due in 2029.
Merz’s eroding support has created a sense of instability in Europe’s top economy, which is struggling with deindustrialisation, sluggish growth and soaring energy costs.

If the AfD’s surge led Merz to abandon the chancellery prematurely, it would give the far right further momentum as France, Italy, Spain and Poland head into elections next year with nativist parties on the march.
after newsletter promotion

Germany has high constitutional hurdles to replacing a chancellor against their will and any appointed successor would need to demonstrate a ruling majority. A failure to do so could trigger a new election.

The AfD is the biggest opposition force in parliament and is leading national opinion polls with about 30%. It has called for Germany to quit the euro, end support for Ukraine and carry out mass deportations of “irregular” migrants, while citing the “destruction” of the CDU as one of its central goals.

The CDU’s debacle in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania – a small, relatively poor state – is particularly bitter for Merz as it was home to the constituency of his arch-rival, Angela Merkel. While she governed Germany for 16 years, Merz appears to be on the ropes after no more than 16 months.

blocks.caption: Elif Eralp (centre), the candidate for Die Linke in Berlin, reacts to the projected results of the state election. Photograph: dts News Agency Germany/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Merz took office in May 2025 at the helm of a coalition with the centre-left Social Democrats (SPD) promising to restore the German economy to strength and slash the AfD’s support.

A failure to make decisive headway on either front has produced profound disappointment in his leadership, with only one in 10 Germans saying they are satisfied with his performance. An inability to connect with voters appears particularly marked in the former communist east, where the AfD is strongest.

In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the Social Democratic party state premier, Manuela Schwesig, distanced herself during the campaign from a key pension change backed by her party in Merz’s coalition government.

She was expected to hold on to power in a left-leaning coalition even if the AfD came out on top when all the votes were counted. Despite leading the polls for months, the far right failed to garner enough support to govern alone and the remaining parties have ruled out working with it.

A confirmed win by Die Linke in Berlin, where the far-left party has called for expropriation of corporate landlords to fight rising housing costs, could see its candidate, Elif Eralp, become the capital’s first leader of Turkish origin.

articles.title: Germany's Merz vows to press on with reforms despite state election losses to far-right AfD
articles.summary: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz suffered a bruising electoral setback in two state elections on Sunday, including a historic defeat for his party, but vowed to press ahead with potentially painful…

image.caption: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz speaks at a news conference in Berlin on Sunday. Merz acknowledged his party's election result as a 'disaster.' (Markus Schreiber/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz suffered a bruising electoral setback in two state elections on Sunday, including a historic defeat for his party, but vowed to press ahead with potentially painful reforms to Europe's biggest economy.
'What needs to be done now requires backbone,' chancellor says

Exit polls by public broadcaster ARD on Sunday night indicated that Merz's centre-right Christian Democratic Union, or CDU, came in with just five per cent in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania — the lowest result ever since the Second World War for the party in any state. The anti-migration, Russia-friendly Alternative for Germany (AfD) party made significant gains Sunday.

Merz acknowledged his party's result as a "disaster" but struck a defiant note, rejecting any retreat from his government's reform agenda. He argued that Germany's economic and political problems made difficult and potentially unpopular reforms more urgent, not less, and pledged to press ahead.

"What needs to be done now requires backbone, steadfastness and patience," Merz said in a statement shortly after the exit polls were announced on public television. "I will demonstrate these qualities as chairman of the CDU and, above all, as chancellor of our country."
In Berlin, the CDU was projected to come in second with 20 per cent, behind the Left party at 24.5 per cent, according to ARD's exit poll.
AfD win seen as big victory for far right politics in Germany

Merz's authority was already damaged by CDU's stinging defeat to AfD in the Sept. 6 election in the small eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt. That result shocked many Germans who had believed their country had developed an immunity to nationalism and assertions of racial superiority after confronting the horrors of its Nazi past through education and laws to outlaw persecution.

Merz, 70, became Germany's leader 16 months ago with promises to turn around an economy that has barely grown in years, but he has failed to lift a sullen national mood and has himself become deeply unpopular.

items: Far-right victory in German state expected to send shockwaves throughout the world

blocks.text: The strong showing of AfD in the Saxony-Anhalt election, where it has best chance yet of forming the country's first far-right regional government since the Second World War, has further weakened the chancellor's standing on the national level as well. In the past two weeks, there have been calls even from within his own party to replace him as chancellor, although no top-level allies have called publicly for his departure, and many have warned against "personnel debates."

Apparently anticipating a tough post-election period, Merz abandoned a planned trip to New York next week to attend the UN General Assembly. Despite the strong headwinds, he has repeatedly said that he's determined to stay on and finish his term as chancellor.

articles.title: Greek police investigate death of 82-year-old man after beach brawl over sunlounger
articles.summary:
Row at resort on Athenian riviera escalated into violence after two elderly bathers reportedly argued over shortage of loungers

Greek police are investigating the death of an 82-year-old man…

blocks.text: Greek police are investigating the death of an 82-year-old man after a brawl over a sunlounger at a beach on the Athenian riviera.

The man had arrived at the popular bathing spot of Vouliagmeni before 10am on Sunday hoping to secure a sunbed, but he soon began arguing with a fellow bather – described by authorities as a “76-year-old man unknown to him” – when it became clear loungers were in short supply.
The row quickly degenerated into a scuffle as others reportedly joined in. The victim, who was with his wife, is believed to have suffered a cardiac arrest during the fight.

“It seems that people who were with [the assailant] also participated,” ERT, the country’s state broadcaster, reported. “The 82-year-old was seriously injured, and needed to be transferred by ambulance to Asklepieion hospital in Voula.
“Despite the efforts of doctors, at around 11am the elderly man succumbed to his wounds.” A post-mortem was immediately ordered.
Police arrested the 76-year-old and, initially, a 21-year-old woman who was with him. The beach resort’s manager was also detained for questioning.

“The incident is under investigation,” said a source, describing the fight as unprecedented. “In Greece disagreement is expressed vocally, with a lot of screaming and shouting, not in fistfights like this – especially between two elderly men. I think that’s why it is so shocking.”

Like other parts of Europe, Greece is undergoing a severe cost of living crisis that has heightened tensions and put strain on social relations. An increase in domestic violence and other disputes has been partly blamed on the pressures of everyday life.

In recent years, there has been growing anger over private rental outfits hogging prime coastal areas with exorbitantly priced sunloungers in Greece, where the sea has an important place in national identity.
Authorities said “all those” involved in the incident would appear before a magistrate.

articles.title: House Republican doubles down on jab at Trump’s immigration enforcement
articles.summary:
Florida’s María Elvira Salazar warns Trump that advisers are ‘compromising his legacy’ and not showing ‘whole picture’

María Elvira Salazar, the

blocks.text: María Elvira Salazar, the Republican congresswoman who has accused the president of going too far on immigration enforcement, doubled down on her criticism of the administration on Sunday, warning Donald Trump that some of his advisers were “compromising his legacy”.

In an interview with CBS News’s Face the Nation, the Florida representative who is locked in a tight race for re-election pleaded with the US president not to “squander” his relationship with Hispanic voters. Though she couched her remarks as criticism of top administration advisers, it was clear that her focus was on Trump’s much-vaunted ambition to carry out the largest mass deportation of undocumented immigrants in US history.
“I’m forewarning him and advising him as a member of Congress from the south Florida area that some of his advisers are just not presenting the whole picture,” she said.

Asked by Face the Nation whether she were referring to Tom Homan, Trump’s “border czar”, or Stephen Miller, the White House deputy chief of staff who has spearheaded the removal of undocumented children, Salazar placed the onus on Trump. “He is the only elected official in the White House. He is the one who has to determine who he listens and who he does not listen to. He is the president.”

Last week Salazar became a rare voice of internal criticism within the Republican party towards Trump when she released a 30-second advert pointing out that even law-abiding undocumented immigrants were getting caught up in the aggressive federal sweep. The ad said: “In July, 50% of the 50,000 people that were detained had no criminal record. Be careful what your advisers are telling you about immigration policy … The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today.”

Salazar’s warning has been backed up by a slew of recent opinion polls that show many Hispanic voters who helped re-elect Trump in 2024 are now turning away from him. They are being repulsed by the rising cost of living and concern about his handling of the economy, as well as by the hardline immigration drive that has led to many hardworking, taxpaying undocumented immigrants being rounded up, detained and deported.

In her CBS News interview, Salazar described herself as “a proud Republican”. “I’m first-generation American, and I want to preserve the American values that are entrenched in the [Republican party] and that the Hispanics share”.

She is currently facing a tough re-election battle in her Miami-area district against her Democratic challenger, Eliott Rodriguez, despite having won in 2024 by 20 points. Trump also won the district by 15 points that year.

Salazar told CBS News that 70% of Americans wanted to see some type of immigration reform. She also pushed back on the administration’s deportation of all undocumented immigrants irrespective of their criminal status.
“The average America understands the difference between the narco and the nanny, and the gangster and the gardener.”
after newsletter promotion
On Saturday, Trump responded to Salazar’s criticisms, saying: “She obviously doesn’t have a very strong feeling about the border. I do.” He added: “Without me, she wouldn’t have gotten elected.”

By breaking her silence on immigration, Salazar has put a spotlight on rising fears within Republican circles that the displeasure of Hispanic voters towards the administration’s policies could cost the party dear in November’s midterm elections. Several House seats in Colorado, Florida, Texas, Nevada and other states could be tipped in the Democrats’ favor as a result.

Steve Scalise, the second-most powerful Republican in the US House, acknowledged on ABC News’s This Week that immigration was creating divisions within his party. Asked what he thought of Salazar’s comment that many Hispanic voters feel betrayed, he said: “I don’t necessarily agree with that statement.”

He added: “When you look at what María said, obviously we have a lot of disagreements in Congress … Even among Republicans we have disagreements on how to actually get to the secure border that we have.”

articles.title: German Chancellor Merz vows to stay on despite 'disaster' in state election
articles.summary: Exit polls show damaging losses for Merz's centre-right CDU party in the states of Berlin and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.

blocks.text: Embattled German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has vowed to stay on despite exit polls in two local elections suggesting damaging defeats for his centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party.

In the north-eastern state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the party was projected to only just scrape into parliament, while the AfD was on track to win the most votes. Merz called the result "a disaster".
In Berlin, the ruling CDU was also expected to be beaten by Die Linke (The Left).
Merz is under mounting pressure, with poor approval ratings and rumours he could even be replaced mid-term in a so-called chancellor swap.
Votes took place on Sunday, a fortnight after the CDU saw its vote halved as the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) won a major victory in the state of Saxony-Anhalt.
Polls for both states closed at 18:00 local time (17:00 BST), with a final result expected in the coming hours.

According to public broadcaster ZDF, the AfD was projected to take 38% of the vote share in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. However, it is unlikely to govern in the state as other parties refuse to work with it.
For Berlin, the broadcaster put the CDU on 20% of the vote share when polls closed, behind Die Linke on nearly 26%.
Prior to Sunday's elections, there had been intense speculation in Germany that Merz could be replaced unless his party's political fortunes improved.
Earlier this week, the leaders of eight German states backed Merz, who has only held the post for 16 months.
This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

articles.title: Baltic spy chiefs warn Moscow is preparing for more decisive action in Europe
articles.summary:
Exclusive: intelligence officers warn campaign against Nato could intensify ‘in months, not years’ – but panic will play into Kremlin psy-ops

European intelligence officials have raised the…
articles.byline: Shaun Walker in Prague and Riga

blocks.text: European intelligence officials have raised the possibility of an imminent Russian test of Nato, with one saying a potential attack could come in a matter of “months not years”.

The warnings came after Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, told parliament that intelligence assessments suggest Russia may launch an attack with drones or missiles on Nato territory in the coming months, as part of efforts to prove that “article 5 is more theoretical than practical”.

French president Emmanuel Macron called Tusk’s warnings “sound and well-documented”, and on Friday summoned party leaders and 2027 presidential candidates for an emergency meeting in Paris, where they discussed – among other topics – intelligence of a growing threat from Russia.

The escalation fears come as the UN general assembly convenes in New York later this week, and amid intensifying airstrikes on both sides of Russia’s war on Ukraine. Kyiv hit Moscow and other Russian regions with hundreds of drones and missiles in the early hours of Sunday, in one of its biggest air attacks of the war.

blocks.caption: Russian president Vladimir Putin, pictured here alongside Adm Viktor Liina, commander of Russia’s Pacific fleet. Photograph: Gavriil Grigorov/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: In separate interviews with the Guardian over the past week, in different locations, three European intelligence leaders discussed their views of the potential threat from Moscow.

Michal Koudelka, head of the Czech Republic’s BIS security service, said that as well as increased drone activity, a small-scale invasion of Nato territory that borders Russia could be part of the Kremlin’s plans. “It’s possible. It could involve a limited incursion, false flag provocations, a massive influence campaign,” he said, in a rare interview at the agency’s headquarters in Prague. He said this scenario could play out in a matter of “months, not years,” but added that “a lot of people are doing everything they can to make sure this doesn’t happen”.

Officials in the three Baltic nations, which border Russian territory, have been more cautious about the prospect of an invasion or other serious escalation, citing Moscow’s currently stretched resources in Ukraine and warning that playing up the prospect of a massive attack might be to play into the Kremlin’s hands.

“We don’t see indications of an imminent attack,” said Normunds Mežviets, director general of the VDD, Latvia’s state security service, in an interview at the agency’s headquarters in Riga. He conceded that there are signs that Moscow is making preparations for more decisive action in Europe, but said it was not clear whether the plans are simply part of a destabilisation strategy.
“It’s still an open question if they have direct and concrete plans or if it’s just within the context of their overall attempts to spread fear and uncertainty in western society,” he said.

blocks.caption: Michal Koudelka, director of the Czech Republic’s Security Information Service (BIS). Photograph: CTK/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.

blocks.text: Baltic politicians, who for many years criticised western Europe for being soft on Russia, now find themselves in the strange position of telling some western leaders to calm down in their public messaging, fearing that talk of an imminent invasion could prove damaging to their societies and economies.

On Saturday, the secretary general of Estonia’s foreign ministry, Jonatan Vseviov, decried “panic on social media” in recent days about a possible attack. “If there is reason to fear an attack, rest assured: we will make that clear. Until then, keep calm, carry on and support Ukraine,” he wrote on X.

Mežviets said that, overall, it was good thing that western Europe had woken up to the threat from Russia. “Before 2022, we constantly warned our western European partners about the threat from Russia, but most of the time our voices were not listened to. In 2022, the approach of our partners changed, they said it turns out the Balts and the Poles had been right,” he said.

Neither Mežviets nor Koudelka would discuss what specific intelligence may have been obtained about Russia’s supposed planning for the coming months, nor would they comment on whether a surprise trip by CIA director John Ratcliffe to Moscow last month – during which he stopped off in Riga – was partly to warn the Kremlin about the dangers of launching an attack on Nato.

After that visit, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov dismissed rumours of a Russian attack on Nato: “It has nothing to do with reality and nothing to do with the intentions of the Russian Federation,” he said.

blocks.caption: CIA director John Ratcliffe, who made a surprise trip to Moscow last month. Photograph: Jonathan Ernst/Reuters

blocks.text: However, many in Europe will have the build up to the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 in the back of their minds, when US officials repeatedly warned Russia was preparing to invade and the Kremlin repeatedly denied it.

As the full-scale war that ensued approaches its fifth winter, US-led efforts to bring about peace in Ukraine show no signs of success, with both Russia and Ukraine intensifying their drone and missile strikes on each other. Ukraine has destroyed much of Russia’s oil infrastructure, targeting refineries and other facilities over recent months.
after newsletter promotion

Moscow has frequently said that the provision to Ukraine of weaponry, intelligence and military advisers makes western countries participants in the war and legitimate targets, but has so far avoided action that might provoke a coordinated response from Nato. Instead, it has launched what western agencies describe as a campaign of sabotage against targets in countries that are the loudest backers of Ukraine, and one-off incidents apparently meant to test boundaries, such as when more than a dozen drones, flying without ammunition, veered into Polish airspace a year ago.

Koudelka said the current Russian tactic was “escalate to de-escalate”, with the Kremlin keen to push at weak points in western societies to tamp down their support for Ukraine’s war effort. “They believe if they escalate enough then European countries will decide not to support Ukraine,” he said.

blocks.caption: A Russian Shahed drone on display in Kyiv. Photograph: Evgeniy Maloletka/AP

blocks.text: The escalation fears come as the Trump administration makes another attempt to kickstart peace negotiations in Ukraine. As well as the Ratcliffe visit to Moscow, White House envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner also made another trip to Moscow in recent weeks, as well as a first-time trip to Kyiv. While Donald Trump has frequently claimed Russian president Vladimir Putin is interested in a deal, there is scepticism in Europe that the Kremlin has any interest in good-faith negotiations.

“I haven’t seen any signs that there is a serious consideration in Moscow about real negotiations,” said Thomas Nilsson, head of Sweden’s military intelligence and security service, in an interview on the sidelines of a conference in Riga. “My assessment is that they are still thinking that they could achieve their strategic objectives, so they are just playing negotiation theatre,” he added.

All three intelligence bosses said that whatever else happens, Russia’s campaign of sabotage in Europe is likely to intensify in the coming months. Nilsson described as a “gamechanger” the recent armed drone incident at Leipzig airport, which German authorities have attributed to Russian intelligence.

“To have an armed UAV drone sent in to a busy airport in the middle of Europe … If you have attacks that could result in losses of life or losses of very critical infrastructure that have a huge implication for society, I think that is a gamechanger,” he said.

blocks.caption: A Ukrainian soldier engages an incoming jet-powered Shahed drone during a Russian aerial attack on Kyiv in August. Photograph: Libkos/Getty Images

blocks.text: Mežviets said Russia was moving from randomised targeting of sabotage and arson attacks intended to sow panic to specific targets linked to western backing for Ukraine. “We see them looking to attack railway infrastructure, Ukraine support infrastructure. Right now we see a move towards defence industry targets,” he said. “If you do this then the psy-op effect is reached anyway, so you get both things in one,” he added.

Nilsson said there were several goals behind the recent intensification of Russian sabotage activity: to reduce support for Ukraine, to introduce splits in Nato and to alarm European populations. “I think Moscow would love Nato to have endless discussion about Article 4 consultations, but coming up with no actions,” he said.

Koudelka said another effect of the sabotage campaign is the stretch on resources of intelligence services, as doubts often linger even when incidents are caused by other factors. “Now, every fire or every malfunction needs to be investigated by intelligence services as a potential terror attack, and that is a good result for them,” he said.

The queer period drama has been named the most popular audience film of the Oscar-predicting festival

Spanish queer drama La Bola Negra has won this year’s people’s choice award at the…

blocks.text: Spanish queer drama La Bola Negra has won this year’s people’s choice award at the Toronto film festival.

The film, which takes place in 1932, 1937 and 2017, focuses on the lives of interconnected gay men. It premiered at this year’s Cannes film festival with the Guardian’s Peter Bradshaw calling it “handsomely produced, lovingly detailed and confidently constructed” in a four-star review.
After a competitive bidding war after its premiere in May, Netflix picked up the rights and the film will be released later this year.
In a prepared statement, directors Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi said that connecting with Toronto audiences in this way was “the greatest gift we could receive”.
It marks the first foreign language winner of the award since 2011’s Lebanese drama Where Do We Go Now?

The award has come to be used as a predictor of Oscar success with past best picture winners such as Green Book, 12 Years a Slave, Nomadland, Slumdog Millionaire and The King’s Speech all picking it up. Last year’s winner was Chloé Zhao’s Shakespeare drama Hamnet which was nominated for eight Oscars, winning one for best actress Jessie Buckley.
Sylvester Stallone biopic I Play Rocky and disability activism drama Being Heumann were named this year’s runners-up.

For the second year, the international people’s choice award was also handed out with British 80s-set Aids drama Elsinore named as the 2026 winner. Last year’s was given to Park Chan-wook’s darkly comedic thriller No Other Choice.

The Toronto winners come after May el-Toukhy’s suspense drama Woman Unknown won the Golden Lion award at the Venice film festival. At Cannes back in May, Cristian Mungiu’s family drama Fjord won the Palme d’Or.

articles.title: Lib Dems use conference to set out £2bn plan to cut fuel duty
articles.summary: Ed Davey’s party made a series of proposals as concern grows among members that voters don’t know what its policies are or what it stands for

blocks.text: The Liberal Democrats have used their conference to unveil a £2bn plan to cut fuel duty, part of a series of policy proposals intended to tackle worries that not enough voters know what Ed Davey’s party stands for.

The proposal to cut fuel duty by 10p a litre for a fixed three-month period came as polling showed Lib Dem policies are less well known than those of Restore Britain, which only launched as a political party in February and has one MP – Rupert Lowe – to their 71.
Davey will set out the fuel duty idea, along with a reduction in the £3 cap on bus fares to £1 and a 10% reduction in rail fares, in his main speech to the event in Brighton on Tuesday.

Daisy Cooper, the party’s deputy leader and Treasury spokesperson, outlined in her speech on Sunday proposals to create economic growth through closer ties with Europe, part of an existing plan to try to rejoin the EU single market.

In a round of media interviews on Sunday morning, Davey pushed back against the idea that the Lib Dems, who are static in national polling at about 12%, risked being forgotten in the political conversation amid the rise in prominence of the likes of Reform UK and the Greens.
His party, Davey insisted, was making a genuine difference, and not just generating coverage without substance.

“I’m talking about real change, not just talking about the bubbles,” he told the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg show. “We have been winning council elections for eight years in a row. That has never happened before – it’s the most successful period that we’ve had.”

While there is no talk among Lib Dem MPs about anyone challenging Davey, some say they are frustrated that the party’s message is too vague and is not being heard by voters, a phenomenon highlighted in polling by More in Common, which was presented at the conference.

One key finding was widespread uncertainty among many voters about what the Lib Dems stood for. Just 39% said they had an idea of this, lower than that for every other major party, including Restore Britain, which was formed just over a year ago by Lowe after he split from Reform UK.

Other parts of the research showed that just 16% of voters said they had heard from the Lib Dems in recent months, against 66% for Reform, while 3% said they had seen Davey on social media, versus 20% for the Reform leader, Nigel Farage.
One Lib Dem MP told a conference fringe event at which the findings were presented that the party needed to expand the geographical and social range of its messaging.

The More in Common research found that the strongest predictor of support for the Lib Dems was a local branch of the upmarket bakery chain Gail’s, with the party doing five times as well in the 2024 general election in the least deprived parts of the country than the most deprived.
after newsletter promotion

“If we want to be a party of government, then we need to have a message for the whole country, not just parts of it,” said Tom Gordon, the MP for Harrogate and Knaresborough, one of just four Lib Dem-held seats in the north of England, against 58 in the south.

Most of Davey’s MPs nonetheless note that he has delivered the party’s best election result for a century, and many expect this total to grow further at the next election even though they have flatlined in national polls, in part due to heavy tactical voting.
But some at the conference do privately say they would like a bit more. “The voters only seem to properly notice us once every four years, when there’s an election,” one longtime party activist said.
“It’s a bit like being curling at the Winter Olympics – the rest of the time we’re forgotten. It would be good if we had a more distinctive message, and that needs boldness.”

articles.title: Senate tackles today VP impeachment vote threshold
articles.summary: Senators are expected to go into caucus today in an attempt to resolve the question on the conviction threshold for Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial.

blocks.text: September 21, 2026 | 12:00am
Retired Chief Justice Artemio Panganiban presented his views on the voting threshold issue during his appearance before the Senate impeachment court as one of the amici curiae, September 16, 2026.
Senate of the Philippines
MANILA, Philippines — Senators are expected to go into caucus today in an attempt to resolve the question on the conviction threshold for Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial.
This comes after the amici curiae (friends of the court) voiced their expert opinions on the matter last week.

Sen. JV Ejercito said the closed-door meeting today would map out whether the dispute over presiding officer Francis Escudero’s ruling would require a vote among senator-judges or if it can be settled through a consensus among the members.
Following the caucus, the Senate impeachment court is scheduled to hear oral arguments from the prosecution and defense panels on Wednesday regarding the disputed voting base.

While Escudero announced earlier that a vote would commence after the oral arguments, Ejercito said he planned to request a deferral of the vote to give senators adequate time to study the constitutional arguments presented by both sides and the amici curiae.

“I will ask for a few days just to absorb this, so that it can be studied, because first of all, I’m not a lawyer. I’ll ask for time so I can absorb all arguments,” Ejercito told radio dzBB yesterday.
Despite this, Ejercito agreed that the Senate should resolve the threshold dispute relatively early in the trial rather than deferring it until judgment day.

Last week, former chief justice Artemio Panganiban, speaking as amicus curiae, said the Senate may skip its vote to resolve the forthcoming deadlock on the “16” voting threshold to convict Vice President Duterte if Escudero simply “changes his mind” and reverses his initial ruling.
Escudero, however, rejected the idea and argued that it would only invite further delays and appeals from the floor.

Panganiban, as well as fellow former chief justices Reynato Puno and Hilario Davide all maintained that the two-thirds threshold to convict Duterte is not fixed at 16 of the 24 senators, saying the decision ultimately lies with the Senate.
Several members of the Senate minority expressed their opposition to a lowered voting threshold.

“If we will revise and vote anew on the threshold, why didn’t we first revise our own rules in order to defend the right of our (absent) members to be able to join the (impeachment) proceedings?” Sen. Robinhood Padilla asked.
Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano, meanwhile, warned of a mistrial if the court changes its rules mid-trial.
“I don’t want to have a mistrial. I don’t want all the work done in this trial to be thrown away,” he said in a Facebook livestream.

Aside from Sen. Ronald dela Rosa, who is in hiding due to a standing arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court, others who may be ineligible to vote are Senators Jinggoy Estrada and Rodante Marcoleta, who are both in jail. Meanwhile, Sen. Loren Legarda has yet to return to the country following an extended medical leave.
At the same time, Ejercito bared that the Vice President has yet to confirm her attendance at the upcoming Senate deliberations for her office’s proposed P785.2-million budget for 2027.
He said the Office of the Vice President (OVP)’s budget hearing, alongside the Office of the President’s, would be scheduled last due to the chamber’s tight calendar as an impeachment court.

Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian previously set ground rules for the OVP budget hearing, clarifying that lawmakers would strictly avoid topics related to Duterte’s ongoing impeachment trial, including the alleged misappropriation of P612.5 million in confidential funds at the OVP and the Department of Education.

articles.title: Passage of school safety law pushed
articles.summary: The Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM 2) is pushing for the passage of a Comprehensive School Safety Act after the recent school violence in South Cotabato, which resulted in the…

blocks.text: Headlines
September 21, 2026 | 12:00am
Police forensic experts sift through the scene of the deadly gun rampage on September 18, 2026, inside a school campus in Banga, South Cotabato.
Philstar.com / John Unson

MANILA, Philippines — The Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM 2) is pushing for the passage of a Comprehensive School Safety Act after the recent school violence in South Cotabato, which resulted in the deaths of three students and wounding of eight others.
In a statement, EDCOM 2 expressed its sympathy to the families in South Cotabato affected by the shooting incident at the Banga National High School (BNHS) on Friday.

“We stand in solidarity with the families, teachers and classmates at Banga National High School in South Cotabato following the shooting on campus. We honor the lives of the students lost, stand with the injured as they recover, and acknowledge the trauma this violence has inflicted on the entire community,” the commission said.
It added that the sorrow brought about by the incident sharpened their resolve to push for action to protect students.
“As stewards of education and policy, we are bound to turn grief into immediate, actionable safeguards across our education system,” EDCOM 2 added.

It called for the passage of the Comprehensive School Safety Act. Enacting this legislation will mandate standardized physical security, access control, and inter-agency threat monitoring across all learning spaces.

The commission also asked for the strict monitoring in the enforcement of the Anti-Bullying Act Implementing Rules and Regulations, and empower Learning Formation Officers in order to have proactive child protection, conflict resolution and student support in schools.

Mental health care through school counsel associates should be expanded. The commission believes that by deploying guidance counselors, speeding up the hiring of SCAs, and setting up support systems would be helpful to students.

It advocated for tightening gun control and storage. Strictly enforcing the mandatory safe-storage laws and holding gun owners legally accountable could prevent minors and unauthorized individuals from acquiring firearms.

Lastly, digital safeguards should be strengthened. EDCOM 2 said that advancing bicameral digital protection through legislation and cyber-safety education would help shield students from online risks, violence and predatory exposure.
The Department of Education yesterday said it would be checking on risks and vulnerabilities in every school.
Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla urged parents to closely monitor their children’s internet and social media activity.

PNP chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. said police would partner with the DepEd and DILG under the initiative of Education Secretary Sonny Angara to conduct comprehensive, site-specific security audits in all public schools.
In Bulacan, the Provincial Peace and Order Council has passed two resolutions to enhance school safety protocols in the province. — John Unson, Rainier Allan Ronda, Ramon Efren Lazaro

An undated photo of the Ombudsman office.

MANILA, Philippines — At the minimum, barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan (BSK) officials should have civil service eligibility, as they are “the frontline of service.”
This is Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla’s proposal, following Congress approval of the postponement of the BSK elections to November 2028. The BSKE measure has yet to be signed into law.

“I think because they are at the frontline of service, they should be civil service eligible to make things orderly. We have to start leveling up so that the frontline service of the government is stronger,” he said in “Executive Session” over radio dzRH Saturday.
Remulla also accused some barangay and SK officials of having “pork barrel” or lumpsum allocations, which the Supreme Court already struck down as unconstitutional.
