blocks.text: Michelle Bachelet, a former president of Chile, has withdrawn her candidacy to become the next secretary general of the ⁠UN, ending a ⁠bid ​that had struggled to gain traction among security council members.
Bachelet, 74, announced ⁠her decision in a video posted on Instagram on Saturday, saying: “I will now continue, with the ⁠same determination as always, my international work.”

The two-time Chilean ​president and former ‌UN human ‌rights chief had positioned her campaign around defending multilateralism and ‌international law at a time when she said both were under sustained pressure.

Bachelet’s exit leaves seven candidates in the race to succeed the secretary general, António Guterres, who will conclude his second five-year term on ‌31 December. It is still possible for more candidates to enter the contest.
Her ​withdrawal comes after a third informal straw poll, held on Friday, showed her support had all but collapsed. That same poll put Costa ⁠Rica’s Rebeca Grynspan in the lead.

The UN security ​council ​will formally recommend ​a single candidate to the 193-member general ​assembly for election. ‌The assembly’s ​approval ​has long been seen as a formality once the council reaches consensus.

articles.title: ‘I have nothing in the UK at all’: British man torn from his Swedish wife and home
articles.summary:
Charles lands at Heathrow with just two bags and nowhere to go as a result of Brexit and Stockholm’s hardline immigration position

Doubled over a Heathrow baggage trolley, the former British…

blocks.text: Doubled over a Heathrow baggage trolley, the former British business director is sobbing uncontrollably, exhausted emotionally and physically after being deported from Sweden.
Hours earlier the 65-year-old had been marched on to a plane in Stockholm, separated from his home and his Swedish wife after a five-year battle to stay in the country after Brexit came to an end.
An only child with no children and no property in the UK, Charles has effectively been made homeless. He was last in the UK in 2022 for one week, and before that not since 2017 when he emigrated.
“I have nothing, nothing in the UK at all,” says Charles as he shows a text from the British consulate explaining where in Heathrow the suddenly homeless can get help.
“All I want is to return to my wife, my home and my friends in Sweden and to live a quiet, peaceful life,” adds Charles, who does not want to publicly share his full identity.

His forced flight on Tuesday shows that deportations of British citizens who lived in Sweden before Brexit are continuing. Stockholm has already deported 458 British people after rejected residency applications, a higher proportion in terms of its population than any EU member state.

blocks.caption: Charles is distraught after landing at Heathrow. Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian

blocks.text: The situation persists despite promises from opposition parties now on track to form a government that they will introduce urgent laws to give Britons a second chance to apply for residency.
“I’ve done nothing wrong but feel I’ve been treated like a criminal,” Charles says.

“Since arriving in Sweden nearly nine years ago, I’ve done everything I can to integrate myself into Swedish society. I’ve learned some basic Swedish, contributed to Swedish society and the Swedish economy, and for that, I’m being punished. Why are they doing this to good, honest, hard-working people like me and my wife?”
Shortly after disembarking in London, he is sitting down in an airport cafe processing what has just happened.

Pointing to a small holdall and a large reusable shopping bag, he says: “All I have is what my wife packed in my bag here with clothes and my little bag” in which he has belongings handed back to him by the captain as he got off the plane.
The bag includes a plastic envelope sealed and emblazoned with the words Kriminalvården, the Swedish Prison and Probation Service, containing meagre belongings.
In it is a miniature tube of toothpaste, a toothbrush and earplugs given to him in the detention centre where he was locked up for two weeks.

blocks.caption: A bag containing a toothbrush, toothpaste and earplugs that was given to Charles in the Swedish detention centre where he was locked up for two weeks. Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian

blocks.text: There is also a bright yellow envelope handed to him by the captain before disembarking which he opens for the first time.

One is a police document saying he does not need to be “escorted”. The other says he is being deported over a failed residency application under the Aliens Act – his latest legal attempt to stay in Sweden after a pre-Brexit residency application, made on time, was rejected.
Charles’s plight started just over two weeks ago when he and his wife received a text requesting that they come to their local police station to discuss their migration case.
They thought it was to discuss their five-year battle to persuade authorities they were in the country lawfully before Brexit. But he was immediately detained and told he would be deported.
“It was an incredible shock. I was distraught. This is not about leaving Sweden, this is about me being forced to leave my wife and my house. They are separating me from my wife,” he said.
“They said we think that if we don’t detain you you will abscond from Sweden because you are not co-operating.
“For the last nine years, all we’ve done is cooperate with them.” He said he begged authorities not to detain him, telling them he would go of his own accord but they said no.
He asked if he could drive back to the UK “so at least I could take some belongings with me because I have nothing in the UK, and they said ‘no, the decision has been made’”.

blocks.caption: A document envelope issued by the Swedish police authority. Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian

blocks.text: Before Brexit, British citizens could live, work, study or retire in any other member state. Under EU law deportation was reserved for exceptional cases of criminality such as terrorism.

After Brexit, Britons and EU citizens who had exercised those free movement rights were told their rights to remain in their host country would be guaranteed in the legally binding withdrawal agreement.

Campaign group British in Europe has raised concerns about the hardline treatment in Sweden for years but this summer it became an election issue after a series of controversial cases emerged, including a removal order issued to a 78-year-old British widow, Joyce Thomas, who had been in the country for 21 years.

blocks.caption: Charles looking for help at Heathrow. Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian

blocks.text: A 74-year-old British man with dementia in full-time care was also ordered to leave after 25 years while another British man, 34, in the country since he was 10 years old, was deported in January.
The cases raised questions about whether Sweden’s hardline immigration position had infected decision-making relating to Britons there before Brexit, a cohort with special protection.
Charles says the experience has been humiliating, particularly as he spent a career in public service helping prisoners and unemployed people to start up businesses.

“When I first moved to Sweden, I thought it was a wonderful place to live. Clean air. We were very close to the sea. Forests, nature, the people that I met when I first moved there were all generally very nice people. That did change,” he said.
“Only two friends know what’s happened in the last couple of weeks. And they’re disgusted by it. One of them said, ‘I’m ashamed, I’m ashamed of what we’ve done to you’.”

blocks.caption: Charles leaves Heathrow airport, heading into an uncertain future. Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian

blocks.text: Jane Golding, chair of British in Europe, says “it is another case that raises the question of whether Swedish implementation is in line with the spirit of the withdrawal agreement,” referring to the legally binding treaty that Michel Barnier, then the EU’s chief negotiator on Britain’s exit from the EU, and Boris Johnson, the then prime minister, promised would protect EU citizens in the UK and British citizens in the EU.
“This British man who has sufficient means and a home and a Swedish wife in Sweden now faces homelessness in the UK where he has nothing,” she says.
“This wasn’t the intention of the EU and UK negotiators of the agreement who said that citizens should broadly be able to continue their lives as before,” she adds.
She also points out that, unlike the UK, there is no statutory body in any member state to oversee correct implementation of the withdrawal agreement.

“Monitoring and support resources for UK citizens in the EU trying to enforce their rights are not commensurate with those in the UK, where there is a dedicated independent monitoring authority. Unfunded volunteers trying to help are overwhelmed,” says Golding.

articles.title: From 'The World’s Greatest Lover' to 'The Happy Jogger': The people who walked across Canada before Terry Fox
articles.summary: Terry Fox may be the most famous person to attempt to cross Canada on foot, but he wasn’t the first, writes Ainsley Hawthorn.

image.caption: Terry Fox may be the most famous person to attempt to cross Canada on foot, but he wasn’t the first, writes Ainsley Hawthorn. (Terry Fox Foundation)

blocks.text: Nfld. & Labrador
Terry Fox may be the most famous person to attempt to cross Canada on foot, but he wasn’t the first, writes Ainsley Hawthorn.
Some cross-Canada trekkers were, like Fox, raising awareness for a cause, others were accused of being frauds

When Terry Fox set off to run across the country, he inspired millions with his dream of curing cancer and his call for others to pick up where he left off after a recurrence of his own illness forced an early end to his Marathon of Hope in August 1980.
Fox may be the most famous person to attempt to cross Canada on foot, but he wasn’t the first.
This weekend, as millions of people around the world prepare to take up Fox’s torch and run to raise money for cancer research, here are the stories of some other cross-Canada trekkers.
One of the earliest, Percy Beresford Greathead, planned to walk not only across Canada but around the world.

Born in England in 1862, Greathead led a colourful life. He was educated in Belgium, lived in the West Indies, South and Central America, and moved to Winnipeg to work as a translator after being mistaken for Jack the Ripper in Whitechapel.
On March 2, 1895, he left Vancouver carrying nothing but a clean pair of socks, a revolver, and some chewing tobacco.

On his solitary travels through the wilderness, he evaded a wild cat by jumping off a cliff, landing safely in moss and brush below. Awakened one night by a grizzly, he put a bullet in its head and ate it the next morning for breakfast.
Greathead had his closest shave when a train came barreling towards him on a narrow railway bridge over a ravine.
“Quick as chained lightning,” he said, “I swung myself over the side and hung there suspended in space until the train had passed by…. I doubt not that during that time some of my hair turned grey.”
He arrived in Halifax on March 27, 1896, and marked his achievement by emptying a bottle of water he had filled from the Pacific Ocean into the Atlantic.
The one problem with Greathead’s incredible story is that he was the only person telling it, and he may not have been a reliable narrator.

An Ontario newspaper announced his arrival in Ottawa in September 1895, only to publish a follow-up a month later calling him a “fakir and fraud” who had run out on his debts in Winnipeg after serving a prison sentence for forgery.
Later cross-country walks were monitored more closely.
Billing himself as “The World’s Greatest Lover,” Burnest Heard pushed an oil drum in front of him the whole way to prove he didn’t hitchhike.
When Charles Burkman and Sid Carr set out to walk from Halifax to Vancouver in 1921, the Halifax Herald offered to sponsor them in return for the right to publish their daily updates from the road.
The publicity attracted others with a taste for adventure, and soon the 1921 walk turned into a race.
Father-son duo Jack and Clifford Behan reached Vancouver first, on June 11, but young married couple Jennie and Frank Dill, who left Halifax a week after the Behans, finished the hike most quickly.
The Dill’s 134-day time was declared “a world’s record” by the Herald and created a sensation, not least because it had been achieved by a woman.

items: Wolves, winter and frostbite: Why 2 Nova Scotians walked to Vancouver in 1921

blocks.text: Frank, in fact, credited Jennie with setting the pace. Before they left Halifax, she had reportedly told him not to worry about the walk “because if he got tired, I’d pick him up and carry him.”
Soon, cross-Canada hikers began using their journeys to raise awareness of social issues.
In 1923, nearly sixty years before Fox’s Marathon of Hope, two other leg amputees walked to advocate for Canadians with disabilities.

Calgarians George Hincks and Marshall McDougall had lost their legs to battlefield injuries during the Great War. Hincks said they were trekking from Calgary to Ottawa "to prove that an amputation case has as much stamina as the average citizen who has not lost a faculty."

items: The forgotten trek across Canada of two WW I veterans who were amputees

blocks.text: Cross-Canada walkers from Greathead onwards financed their journeys by selling picture postcards of themselves or giving talks along the way.

Hincks and McDougall used their lectures to describe how disabled Canadians were shut out of the job market. Hincks himself had been unemployed for three years, and, according to historian Eric Story, the men placed the onus on their able-bodied audiences to overcome their prejudices and stop judging by appearances.
Hiking on crutches eventually rubbed their feet, hands, and underarms raw, and the pair were forced to call off their walk in western Ontario. Hincks, like Fox, stopped in Thunder Bay.
Four decades later, Ken Weldrick also crossed the country for disability rights.
Calling himself “The Happy Jogger,” the 23-year-old child welfare worker ran from Vancouver to St. John’s to raise awareness and funds for Canadians with intellectual disabilities.

“In the larger cities like Toronto and Montreal,” he said. The associations for people with intellectual disabilities "have a lot of money, and the patients can get the care they need. But in the other parts of the country, there are not enough funds coming in.”
Weldrick mostly slept outdoors and followed a routine of running for half an hour, resting for five minutes, then running again.
Undertaking the trip in the middle of winter, he was hospitalized in Manitoba for two months after suffering serious frostbite to his face, hands, and feet. He lost all his toenails as a result.
By the time he reached St. John’s on July 1, 1975, supporters had pledged about $7,000 directly to local charities for people with intellectual disabilities.
There are people walking across Canada right now. Though it may be a pastime almost as old as Confederation, the prospect of crossing this great continent on foot hasn’t lost any of its appeal.

articles.title: 'Agent Layla': Sex assault victim turned secret agent brings her abuser to justice
articles.summary: A new CBC Podcast tells how Vienna Luke, the victim of a historic sexual assault, went undercover as an RCMP agent to record a confession from the family member who assaulted her years earlier.

image.caption: With the support of her sister Shawnessy Luke(left), Vienna Luke became a police agent in her own case. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

blocks.text: WARNING: This article may affect those who have experienced​ ​​​sexual violence or know someone affected by it.
On a Friday morning in 2021, just a couple of days before Halloween, Vienna Luke zipped up an oversized puffer jacket with a big hood, and put on sunglasses to hide her face.
In a SUV outside her home, plainclothes RCMP officers waited to whisk her away on a secret mission — a face-to-face meeting with the man responsible for the worst night of her life.

Luke, a fitness instructor and mother of two children, was the key undercover agent in an RCMP operation that — if successful — could lead to the rarest of outcomes: a criminal conviction in a sexual assault that that had occurred 14 years earlier.
If Luke failed, her case and the truth about what had happened that night would almost surely be lost to time.
The police referred to Luke using a code name: Agent Layla.
CBC has obtained the surreptitious recording of that mission. It shows an extremely rare instance of RCMP turning the victim into an agent in her own case.
The RCMP sergeant who led the investigation say it’s an approach that is almost never tried — especially in sexual assault cases.
"For the victim to have the strength, and the investigative team [to have the] determination[...] is almost unheard of," said Sgt. Joëlle LaChance.

Facing the man who assaulted her, her estranged brother-in-law, "Agent Layla" presses him for answers over the course of 70 minutes. Luke ultimately elicits a confession that surpassed even the highest hopes of the RCMP team gathered in a nearby hotel room listening in over a wire. The breakthrough was so moving that it brought tears to a hardened undercover officer accustomed to working with drug dealers and murderers.
"She literally took her life back in her hands," said one of the officers from the undercover unit, working with LaChance.
"There wasn’t a dry eye in that room," said LaChance.

That recording — along with interviews from Luke, her middle sister Shawnessy Luke, and the police officers involved in the sting — is part of a new four-part CBC podcast called Personally: Agent Layla.

The podcast details how Luke managed to get the truth, put the man who assaulted her behind bars, and begin to heal from an incident that left her traumatized, detached from her own body, and at odds with members of her family who at times failed to take her side.
A night with only one memory

At 20 years old, Luke was living at home with her family in the Vancouver suburbs after attending a Bible school overseas. Her life had been sheltered; she says she had never been kissed, or even held hands with a man.

While she contemplated her future, she decided to move in with her eldest sister, brother-in-law and their sons in the small B.C. town of Fort St. John — a 14-hour drive north from where she was raised.

Her brother-in-law, Justin Sewell, was a respected veterinarian who was active in a local Christian church. Sewell was 11 years older than her and he had been a trusted member of the family since Luke was a child.
During a week when Luke's sister and nephews were out of town, Sewell proposed a plan. He suggested she get drunk for the first time at home with him, in what he described as a "safe place."
Luke says she had heard of another Christian girl who had done something similar to experiment for the first time with drinking, so she went along with his idea.
WARNING: This story contains graphic details about sexual abuse.
According to testimony presented in court and extensive interviews conducted by the CBC, Luke only sipped the cocktails he made — one of them a Kahlua-based "Brown Cow."

As she and Sewell danced to country music in the living room, Luke remembers her legs buckling. As the world went black, she felt nauseous and thought to herself that drinking alcohol didn’t seem so fun after all.
Aloud, she spoke a phrase that only drives home how naive she was to what was about to happen.
"I just love Jesus," she said. "I just love Jesus. And then I was out."

For Luke, everything about the rest of that night is blank, except for one memory that would both torment her and propel her to seek accountability in the almost two decades to come: a brief moment when she says she awoke mostly naked in her bed.
"I was looking at myself, from above, to my brother-in-law taking off my underwear," she said.
'We gotta tell mom and dad'

In the aftermath of that horrible evening, Luke says she tried to "shelve" what happened. For months, she fought what she described as a war between her body that remembered, and her brain trying to forget.

She moved back home to her parents’ home near Vancouver and didn’t come face-to-face with Sewell again until half-a-year later at Christmas when the entire family went to Florida for a cruise. But when they said their goodbyes at the airport, her middle sister, Shawnessy Luke, noticed something was off.
"I remember it like it was yesterday," Shawnessy Luke said. "The way he hugged her. And I think that’s strange. That’s prolonged. And I knew something was going on."

Shawnessy Luke describes herself as a person with great intuition and "like a dog with a bone." She waited until she and Vienna Luke got back to their parent’s home to ask questions. She was doing her laundry in the family’s narrow utility room when she insisted that her sister explain.
"She definitely pulled it out of me," said Vienna Luke. "I did not volunteer."

Vienna Luke told her sister what happened in the days leading up to the drinking game, facts that were accepted in court: How Sewell had held her hand, how he called her up from her basement bedroom to watch a lightning storm and then massaged her back, and how he told her he loved her.
Then she shared how Sewell proposed she get drunk, and how she couldn’t remember much more than that.

"In my moral compass brain, the minute I heard those things, I was like, I don’t need to know anymore, I believe you," said Shawnessy Luke. "We’ve got to tell someone about this because [...] whatever happened to you [...] was wrong."
Shawnessy Luke says she insisted they tell their mom and dad.

The night in question had happened in June 2007, about 10 years before the #MeToo social movement. As Vienna Luke told her parents about Sewell holding her hand and massaging her back, she stopped short of sharing the most damning memory of all — that she woke up to Sewell removing her underwear. She felt like her parents didn’t know how to handle what she was saying, and didn't have the vocabulary at the time to talk about sexual assault.
"I knew that I couldn’t share more," she said.
Her father called Sewell right away. She didn’t overhear their conversation, but she recalls her father handed her the phone and she found herself suddenly on the line with Sewell.

Vienna Luke pleaded with Sewell to tell his wife what had happened, hoping her oldest sister would take her side. She still doesn’t know if that happened, only that her oldest sister has continued to stand by her husband and is still married to him today.

Her parents declined to be interviewed for this story. In a victim impact statement filed in court, they wrote: "Our effort to uncover the full story was unsuccessful. Lacking information and clarity, we had no path forward. We felt uneasy about what we knew, but did not pursue this matter further."
Years of numbing

In the years that followed, the Luke family struggled with the divide created by that night: Vienna’s oldest sister and Sewell on one side, Shawnessy and Vienna Luke on the other, and their parents trying to walk a line between all three of their daughters.
"It was easier to take Justin for his word," Vienna Luke said. "He was the one that knew what happened. He got to write the story."

With no clarity about what had actually happened and that one horrific memory of him removing her underwear replaying in her head, Luke says she spent years feeling like a robot trying to numb her pain.
She also moved out of her parent’s house and moved to Vancouver, got a job, and met a man who she credits for showing her how to love herself again.
When they started a family, Luke says something inside her started to shift. She knew she’d have to tell her children the truth someday, and something about birth reconnected her to her body.
"My body wasn’t just laboring," she wrote in her journal. "[It was] waking up."
Twelve years after the assault, and weeks after she delivered her second child, Luke called up her sister Shawnessy.
"Hey, I’m ready to deal with this," she said.
So the two sisters made a list.
The sister detectives
Together, they wrote down all the names of people they suspected had soured on Sewell after he had disclosed to his wife and friends two extramarital affairs five years earlier.
Shawnessy Luke's first call was to one of those ex-lovers, a female veterinarian who had worked at Sewell's clinic.
In a recording of that phone call shared with CBC and in court testimony, the woman said she and Sewell were discussing previous sexual experiences when he said something shocking.

"So what he told me was that he put ketamine in [Vienna’s] drinks," the ex-lover revealed during a phone call Shawnessy Luke recorded. "But he didn’t know how much was enough to like, make her forget."
The sisters say this new information validated a hunch they had come to believe: that Vienna Luke had been drugged.
It also gave her a little piece of evidence to march into the Vancouver Police Department and report.
'I do my job for the victims'

Vienna Luke's file was transferred up to the small RCMP detachment in Fort St. John. Against all odds, it landed on the desk of Sgt. Joëlle LaChance, a female officer with a special commitment to cases that many officers would simply dismiss as too hard and too old.
"My whole life I have been a champion for the underdog," she said. "Being able to stand up for the victim … it's why I do my job."

LaChance said she knew Sewell — with his stellar reputation in the community, had a lot to lose. So instead of going directly to the veterinarian to question him, she called on other RCMP units for help, including the undercover unit.
Together, they hatched a plan.

Court records show Sewell had emailed Vienna Luke several times in the years since the night of the drinking game, asking her to accept that he had changed and hoping that the extended family could be together again.

Luke showed the police those emails. Together, they crafted back emails that suggested there could be a possibility for family reconciliation, but first Luke would need the whole truth and they’d have to meet face-to-face.
They pitched Sewell on a plan to fly to Vancouver to meet Luke.
Unbeknownst to Sewell, Luke would be prepared.

For weeks, she trained, preparing to grill him for the facts. She spent a couple of days in a hotel room, sitting across from an undercover RCMP officer who role played with her. The officer worked to get her comfortable asking tough, direct questions, using words like "vagina" and "ejaculate" — specific terms that would be necessary for charges to be laid.
"This isn’t a trained hitman," the undercover officer said. "She’s very polite, very soft-spoken. And I knew that was exactly the opposite of what we were going to need to do."

On the day of the sting at Vancouver airport, everyone involved held their breath. RCMP had laid the groundwork, but as soon as the tape started recording and Sewell walked in, it would be entirely up to Luke to get the truth.
For the plan to work, Luke would need to be both victim and hero. The RCMP believed it was the best chance at bringing charges. Luke knew it was her only chance to get answers.
"You think I'm exactly the same," Luke remembered thinking. "You think I'm gonna play your same little game, but we've got a new game and I'm writing it."
An extraordinary encounter – and as much truth as she’ll ever get
In the recording, Sewell sits down across from Luke and quickly tries to take control. He claims pornography and a culture that objectifies women is part of why he assaulted her that night.
"Okay, but you’re not actually telling me what happened," Luke replies. "Let’s get back to the night and what actually … happened."
The undercover officer who had spent time coaching Luke for this moment felt proud.
"Take control of that conversation," he said in an interview while listening back to the recording. "Don’t just accept a two-minute fluffy bullshit answer."
Luke persists, peppering Sewell with questions seeking specific details, seemingly undeterred by the fact she’s learning this information about the worst night of her life for the first time.

On tape, Sewell confesses to drugging her, removing her clothing, masturbating and ejaculating twice on her body, and taking 30 photos, including ones where he is spooning her naked body and one where his penis is near her face.
As Luke prepares to wrap up, she lobs an open ended question.
"Is there anything that I’m not asking?" Luke said.
"No reason for me to disclose this. But I took pictures of you at other times," Sewell replied.
His response allowed the RCMP to recommend another charge, this one for voyeurism.
A rare conviction in a historic sexual assault
In the morning of April 26, 2022, Fort St. John RCMP arrested Sewell as he left his home for work.

Sewell pleaded guilty to one count of sexual assault and two counts of voyeurism — one for the photos he took of her the night he assaulted her and one for times he had watched her through her bedroom window. Crown agreed to stay a charge of administering a drug with intent to commit a sexual assault.
In the courtroom, Luke’s mother, father, and Sewell’s supporters listened to the recording from the airport.
A provincial court judge sentenced Sewell to house arrest. Crown appealed and the Court of Appeal judges determined the lower court judge had overstated the mitigating fact of Sewell’s confession.
They issued a sentence of 33 months less a day in prison for his crimes.
Luke asked the court to remove the publication ban on her name — something that is standard in cases of sexual assault to protect the victim’s identity.
As she began to tell friends and acquaintances her whole story, that she was the unnamed victim, she says she realized how important it was to her that she could also say she was the secret agent.
"It took this … experiment of the police saying, 'Hey, how about you go undercover as yourself' for me to realize, whoa, look at the advocate I can be for myself," she said.
"I was Agent Layla. That's me."
The CBC podcast Personally: Agent Layla is available wherever you get your podcasts.

If you’re in immediate danger or fear for your safety or that of others around you, please call 911. For support in your area, you can look for crisis lines and local services via the Ending Sexual Violence Association of Canada database. ​​

articles.title: From Beda to UP: James Payosing brings premium spark to UAAP
articles.summary: James Payosing, an NCAA champion and a Finals MVP with the San Beda Red Lions, brings the same winning mentality to the UP Fighting Maroons

blocks.text: PUMPED. James Payosing in action for the UP Fighting Maroons in the UAAP Season 89 men's basketball tournament.
UAAP
James Payosing, an NCAA champion and a Finals MVP with the San Beda Red Lions, brings the same winning mentality to the UP Fighting Maroons

items: James Payosing made a strong debut for the UP Fighting Maroons, scoring 16 points and contributing to their 94-75 victory over the Ateneo Blue Eagles.
Payosing, a former NCAA champion, emphasizes teamwork and aims to bring a winning mentality to UP, filling the void left by key players from previous seasons.
He believes in the importance of each player excelling in their roles to maintain the team's success, as UP currently leads the standings at 2-0.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – James Payosing needed just 15 minutes to show he truly belongs on the UAAP stage.
The former NCAA champion poured in 16 points on 4-of-5 shooting and added 3 rebounds and 2 assists as the UP Fighting Maroons dispatched the Ateneo Blue Eagles, 94-75, on Saturday, September 19.
Payosing did it at the Araneta Coliseum, the same venue where he led the San Beda Red Lions to the NCAA Season 99 championship in 2023 and earned Finals MVP honors.
Now, he is looking to bring that same winning mentality to UP.

“As a player, my mindset is that I’m in a team sport, so I’m just doing my role that complements the team. When one wins, everybody does,” Payosing said after just his second game with UP following his initial commitment in 2024.
“Since this is my first season here in the UAAP, I’m just embracing the games and the opportunity. Whenever I play, I aim to stand out in my role.”
That has always been Payosing’s approach, even during his time at San Beda.

The 6-foot-2 guard knows when to pick his spots, rarely forces the issue, and brings an unrelenting intensity on defense. He does not need the ball in his hands to make an impact, and against Ateneo, that versatility proved valuable.

Payosing helped contain Ateneo’s rookie sensation Kieffer Alas, who was held to just 3 points in the second half. Alas finished with 13 points on 5-of-11 shooting as Ateneo struggled to find answers against UP’s defense.
For Payosing, the performance was another glimpse of what he can bring to a team built around a collective identity rather than one dominant star.
The 23-year-old is also enjoying a rare opportunity to bring glory to two of the country’s proudest collegiate programs over the past five years, San Beda and UP.
“I expect a winning culture here at UP. Winning a championship isn’t easy, but I’ve been preparing for it since last year, my residency year,” Payosing said.

At UP, Payosing is expected to help fill the void left by Harold Alarcon, Reyland Torres, and Terrence Fortea, three key pieces of a Fighting Maroons team that reached the UAAP finals in each of the last five seasons.
Payosing appears to be comfortable with the challenge of filling those shoes.

UP now sits atop the standings at 2-0 after the first week of games, and Payosing hopes his role can help keep the Fighting Maroons on the same path that made them a fixture in the UAAP title picture.
“All I’m saying is that let’s be star players in each of our roles so that when the five of us are on the court, we’re all superstars,” Payosing said.
“The level of competition is almost the same [as the NCAA] and it really comes down the mindset that whoever wants to win the most will win,” he added. – Rappler.com

items: The investigation into NSFWPH began when student journalist Lance Bustos approached the author, leading to months of tracking online behavior and community dynamics within the forum.
The investigation highlighted the challenges of jurisdiction in internet investigations, as harmful sites may operate outside the Philippines, complicating accountability for local authorities.

The most significant aspect of the investigation was connecting with victims of the site, emphasizing the importance of understanding their experiences and shifting the blame from victims to those who violate trust.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
Earlier this year, student journalist Lance Bustos approached me at an event and told me about NSFWPH.
That was how this investigation began.
It sounds simple, but a lot of investigative work starts exactly that way: someone knows something, sees something, or has been watching something for a while, and decides to tell a journalist.

Lance, who would later become a Rappler fellow, had already been looking into NSFWPH for months. He wasn’t just browsing the site. He had been doing OSINT, or open-source intelligence — collecting publicly available information online, making sense of it, and connecting the dots.
You may have heard the term during the Sara Duterte impeachment trial when the National Bureau of Investigation began investigating the Vice President’s threats against President Bongbong Marcos.

In practice, it can be as basic as following usernames, social media posts, links, timestamps, website records, online videos, and other digital crumbs until a pattern begins to emerge. It has become an effective tool for journalists.

In my case, aside from NSFWPH, during the last presidential election campaign, we investigated DDoS attacks against us and other news sites. We followed the digital trail until it led us to one of the people behind the attacks.
With NSFWPH, Lance had already started doing the same thing. When I began working with him, we kept going.

For months, we tracked behavior inside the forum. We documented not just what people posted, but how the community worked, and how members communicated with one another. What earned attention? What behavior was rewarded? What did users brag about? What did they consider normal?
We felt that truly understanding this was important because online communities can shape behavior.

You may remember 8chan, the forum that became notorious after users linked to several mass shootings posted extremist material there before being shut down in 2019. Obviously, NSFWPH is a different case. But the broader point is the same: what gets normalized online can spill into the real world.
And as we’ve written, we found examples of real-world harm, including students who appeared to have been targeted.

After the Tacloban and Zamboanga shootings, whose shooters allegedly had been influenced by malign online forces operating within an amorphous NVE (nihilistic violent extremism) network, it’s only become more important to pierce through these online spaces.
We also looked at how NSFWPH was set up. Using publicly available tools, we found that it was routed through Cloudflare, which made it more difficult to identify the site’s operator.
That led us to another recurring problem in internet investigations: jurisdiction.
A site may target Filipinos and harm Filipinos, but the companies, servers, or operators behind it may be outside the Philippines. Local authorities can quickly hit a wall.

We see versions of this problem with other platforms too, whether the issue involves Roblox, Meta, or other global services. It is one reason authorities have pushed for foreign platforms to have a local legal entity that can be held accountable without having to rely immediately on international cooperation that may take time. New bills in recent months are legislating for exactly this: official local entities for international platforms that can be quickly held accountable.

And yet the most important part of this investigation was not technical. It goes back to the victims themselves, the people most affected. We wanted to find a person who had actually been victimized on the site and was willing to talk.
I eventually came across one who had already shared her experience online and had directly mentioned NSFWPH. I talked to her, and she articulated her experience bravely and well.
She said the shame belonged to the people who spread the material, not to the person who trusted a partner after being promised that those photos or videos would stay private.
Too often, when intimate material leaks, people ask the victim: Why did you send it? Why did you allow yourself to be recorded?
The better question is: Why did someone violate that trust?
Since the investigation came out, more people have started sending us their own cases. We are going through them now and looking at where our reporting can help.

One person came forward with a tip. That tip became months of monitoring and documenting, leading to our final report. The reporting reached victims. And now some of them are coming forward too. It’s a reminder that sometimes that is how an investigation grows, with one person deciding to speak.
Email us at desk@rappler.com. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Should municipalities ban smart glasses in pools and change rooms? We asked a dozen cities
articles.summary: Some city councils are banning smart glasses in public change rooms to prevent people from being covertly recorded, but 10 Canadian municipalities contacted by CBC News say existing rules are…

image.caption: A candidate for Vancouver council wants to see smart glasses banned in city parks and recreation facilities. (Vancouver Park Board/Twitter)

blocks.text: Some city councils are banning smart glasses in public changerooms to prevent people from being covertly recorded, but 10 Canadian municipalities contacted by CBC News say existing rules are sufficient.

In Australia, local councils in Sydney, Brisbane and in the Melbourne area banned them from public pools and change rooms, with one mayor going so far as to call them “pervert glasses” in introducing the motion.
The glasses were also recently banned by a Toronto dance venue.

items: Smart glasses expose a gap in Canadian privacy laws

blocks.text: Caitlin Stockwell, a lawyer running for municipal council in Vancouver, is calling for a similar ban there.
Stockwell noted it’s primarily women, children and gender diverse people who are being covertly recorded and harmed when the videos are posted online.
In the U.K., there are also reports of people asking for money to take the videos down.

“We think if there are extra rules in place that can reduce the likelihood of these glasses being used in that way, that's something that our city hall and park board should be looking into,” Stockwell said.
So far, the idea does not seem to be taking root across the country.

items: Police did not intervene as Canada's most prolific voyeur was 'looking for more victims,' court records show

blocks.text: CBC News reached out to 12 Canadian cities to find out if any were considering a ban.
Ten responded by deadline. Representatives all said existing rules that prohibit the use of recording devices within these facilities also apply to smart glasses.

“The regulations already in effect across all of Montreal's aquatic facilities prohibit taking photos and recording videos inside the pool areas and locker rooms. These rules apply regardless of the type of device used,” a City of Montreal spokesperson said in an emailed statement that was typical of the responses CBC News received.
The City of Ottawa’s policy is under review, according to Tracey McGarry, the city’s director of complexes, aquatics and special services.

“Any updates would further clarify restrictions related to photography, video recording, audio recording, and livestreaming in recreation facilities. We have had no issues with smart glasses in city recreation facilities.”
But Stockwell says more proactive rules are needed because of the covert nature of the glasses.

“The issue that we're seeing that's unique with wearable recording tech is that it's actually really difficult to tell whether they're recording someone or not. So, a more proactive rule in place to restrict the type of harm that they can be used for is to prohibit wearing those glasses in those spaces altogether.”

items: More stories from Vancouver-South Coast

blocks.text: Smart glasses have a light that indicates when they’re recording, but it isn’t always obvious and some people have tampered with it, an issue engineers at Meta, one of the companies developing these glasses, are grappling with.
The idea would be to have signage indicating smart glasses are not allowed in the facilities, Stockwell said.

“Letting people know these glasses are banned, it … increases the likelihood that more people will catch it, as opposed to just the person that's targeted by the filming themselves and might see the video after the fact.”
Lloyd Richardson, director of technology at the Canadian Centre for Child Protection in Winnipeg, says their organization is already seeing children targeted by covert recording.
This was the case before smart glasses, and it's not always clear what type of device was used to make the recordings, but the glasses make it easier to be inconspicuous, he says.
"We've seen what are obviously surreptitious recordings of children in bathrooms. We've seen it in daycares, we've seen it in pools. "
Richardson says he agrees with a ban in municipal facilities, but believes it needs to go further.

"I think we really need to like stand up to sort of sovereign law here and say ... you can't design a device like this. This is privacy invasive. It's harmful. And ... you can't ship them into Canada."
Stockwell says there are change rooms in Vancouver where cellphones aren’t allowed, and she was once reminded by another patron to put her phone away.
The Sydney-area ban excludes people with impairments who use the glasses for accessibility reasons, and Stockwell says she envisions a Vancouver ban having the same exemptions.
Policies
CBC News asked 12 municipalities whether they’re considering a ban on smart glasses in public facilities.
These responses have been edited for length and clarity.

Toronto: For any filming and photography in city parks, recreation facilities and recreation programming, an individual must not engage in filming and photography in washrooms and change rooms and obtain permission from staff prior to taking photographs or filming in active recreation spaces. We continue to review and evaluate our education and enforcement practices. Further refinements to our practices surrounding all filming tools, including smart glasses, will take place as we learn more.

Montreal: The regulations already in effect across all of Montreal's aquatic facilities prohibit taking photos and recording videos inside the pool areas and locker rooms. These rules apply regardless of the type of device used. Additionally, in several of its new facilities, the city has set up universal (or gender-neutral) locker rooms where nudity is not allowed.

Vancouver: The Vancouver Board of Parks and Recreation's pool guidelines state that the use of photographic devices, including cameras and cellphones, in fitness centres, swimming pools, and connected change spaces is not permitted without prior staff approval. While the park board does not currently have a specific policy regarding smart glasses, all patrons are expected to respect the privacy, safety and comfort of others when using our facilities. We continually review emerging technologies and consider their potential impacts on the privacy, safety and experience of patrons using our spaces.

Ottawa: The City of Ottawa’s current policy prohibits the use of electronic equipment with photographic capabilities in change rooms, washrooms, exercise rooms and swimming pool areas. It applies broadly to devices that can capture images or video and is not limited to specific technologies. Smart glasses with photo or video recording capabilities would be subject to the same restrictions as other photographic devices within these areas. The policy is currently under review, and any updates would further clarify restrictions related to photography, video recording, audio recording and livestreaming in recreation facilities. We have had no issues with smart glasses in city recreation facilities.

Edmonton: City of Edmonton recreation facilities prohibit the use of recording devices in change areas. This includes all devices that can record (photograph/picture, video and/or audio) and including, but are not limited to, cellphones, cameras, video recorders, laptops and tablets. Given that smart glasses have recording capabilities, they would also be prohibited in change areas. Recording devices can be brought into the space, but must be turned off and stored out of view (pocket, purse, locker). Patrons must leave the prohibited space before using the recording device, including speaking on the phone or texting.

Winnipeg: Recording devices are not permitted in washrooms, change rooms and locker rooms at City of Winnipeg facilities. We encourage patrons to report any unusual behaviour or the use of recording devices to on-site staff.
Quebec City: Quebec City prohibits the use of all electronic devices that can record, film and photograph in its swimming pools and change rooms. Smart glasses are included in this ban.

Hamilton: While the City of Hamilton does not have a specific bylaw governing the use of smart glasses in municipal recreation facilities, as with any device that may capture photos or video, we expect all facility users to respect the privacy and dignity of others, particularly in washrooms, change rooms and saunas, where photo taking is not permitted.

Kitchener: While the City of Kitchener does not have a bylaw or policy that specifically references smart glasses, we do have an existing policy that prohibits the use of cellphones, cameras, personal digital assistants and other electronic devices with photographic capabilities in change rooms and public washrooms at all city facilities. This policy is posted in all of our municipally operated recreation facilities. Devices with photographic or recording capabilities would generally fall within the intent of the policy. Our focus is on maintaining privacy and ensuring residents feel comfortable and safe when using city facilities, regardless of the type of technology involved.

Halifax: The Halifax Regional Municipality has a policy governing image recording and broadcasting at its recreation facilities, including pools. Recording is strictly prohibited in change rooms, washrooms and similar areas at all municipal recreation facilities. Recording in active recreation spaces, including pools and pool decks, is restricted and requires permission from facility staff. Staff may require consent or waivers from participants and/or parents or guardians. The policy applies to image recording and broadcasting using photographic and modern digital recording technology of any form, means or type.
Calgary and London: No response by deadline.

articles.title: Akbayan welcomes SC decision on anti-political dynasty law
articles.summary: Akbayan Party-list Rep. Chel Diokno on Sunday welcomed the Supreme Court"s (SC) directive for Congress to enact an anti-political dynasty law.

blocks.text: Published September 20, 2026 5:38pm
Akbayan Party-list Rep. Chel Diokno on Sunday welcomed the Supreme Court’s (SC) directive for Congress to enact an anti-political dynasty law.

"This decision of the Supreme Court is groundbreaking. This is a very welcome decision for us because we have long been advocating for a genuine Anti-Political Dynasty Law," Diokno told Super Radyo dzBB.
The SC directed Congress to enact an anti-political dynasty law at the earliest opportunity, ruling that its failure to do so for 39 years constitutes grave abuse of discretion.
The ruling stemmed from consolidated petitions filed by several groups and individuals seeking to compel Congress to fulfill its constitutional duty to enact a law prohibiting political dynasties.

SC spokesperson Camille Ting said the use of the word "shall" in Article II, Section 26 of the 1987 Constitution makes clear that the State has a mandatory duty to prohibit political dynasties. (Supreme Court of the Philippines)
The provision states that the State shall guarantee equal access to opportunities for public service and prohibit political dynasties "as may be defined by law."
The SC, however, said Congress retains the authority to define what constitutes a political dynasty and determine the scope of the prohibition.

Diokno pointed out that the version of the Anti-Political Dynasty Bill filed by their group in the House of Representatives would ban relatives up to the fourth degree of consanguinity or affinity from running for or occupying a public post in the same constituency or jurisdiction.

"The Anti-Political Dynasty Bill that we are pushing covers up to the fourth degree of consanguinity or affinity and includes everyone. For us, all positions, whether local or national, should be covered by the prohibition against political dynasties," Diokno said.

This version differs from House Bill 8389, which the House of Representatives approved on third and final reading in June. The measure prohibits relatives up to the second degree of consanguinity or affinity from running for or occupying a post in the same constituency or jurisdiction.
"An Anti-Political Dynasty Bill with real teeth should be enacted. If only our version in the House had been passed into law, political dynasties would truly be reduced," Diokno said.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: NIA assures sufficient water supply as strong El Niño draws near
articles.summary: The National Irrigation Authority (NIA) said on Sunday that adequate irrigation water is available as a strong El Niño approaches, adding that it will maintain a double dry cropping calendar to…

blocks.text: The National Irrigation Authority (NIA) said on Sunday that adequate irrigation water is available as a strong El Niño approaches, adding that it will maintain a double dry cropping calendar to maximize the dry season.
In an interview with Super Radyo dzBB, NIA Administrator Eduardo Guillen said the agency actually prefers sunny weather, which is why it is implementing double dry cropping.
“Sa pagsasaka po, sa pagtatanim natin, mas gusto nga po ng NIA ‘yung maaraw, kaya nga po binabago ng NIA ‘yung ating cropping calendar, ginagawa po naming… double dry cropping,” Guillen said.
(When it comes to farming, NIA actually prefers sunny weather. That is why NIA is shifting our cropping calendar and implementing… double dry cropping.)

“... Ang ginagawa po ng NIA ngayon, dinadala natin ‘yung ating cropping sa parteng October, aani tayo ng January, tanim ulit tayo ng March [at] aani ulit tayo ng June. So ‘yan po ‘yung tinatawag [na] double dry cropping,” he added.
(What NIA is doing now is shifting our cropping schedule to around October so we can harvest in January, then plant again in March and harvest in June. So that is what we call double dry cropping.)

Guillen pointed out that this system differs from the previous wet and dry cropping calendar, where planting started in November or December, harvest took place in March, and replanting occurred in July.

He explained that sunny weather yields higher crop output through photosynthesis, which relies on sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide. However, he emphasized that a sufficient water supply remains crucial to sustain crop growth.

Citing PAGASA, Guillen said the effects of the strong El Niño are projected to be felt in the last quarter of the year, between October and December, and will persist until the second quarter of 2027.
NIA stated that storing water is one of the key ways the agency prepares, making high dams like Magat Dam in Isabela vital to operations.
Guillen said the Magat Dam is almost full and is expected to supply irrigation to 90,000 hectares of farmland.
Meanwhile, Pantabangan Dam in Nueva Ecija, which supplies water to five areas in Luzon, is also nearly full and capable of irrigating around 120,000 hectares.
High-value crops
As part of its preparations, NIA highlighted the importance of coordination with the Department of Agriculture (DA) to jointly identify areas likely to face water shortages.
“Doon sa mga irrigated areas natin alam po ng NIA kung ilan ‘yung kaya niyang patubigan, na tataniman po natin ng palay. Kasi yung palay matakaw po sa tubig ‘yan,” Guillen said.
(In our irrigated areas, NIA knows how many hectares can be supplied with water for rice production, which requires a substantial amount of water.)

“Now, kaya po sinusulong… ‘yung masusing koordinasyon namin ng Department of Agriculture, dahil po pag na-identify namin ‘yung mga areas na kukulangin po ng patubig, marami naman po tayong pwedeng itanim na high-value crops diyan,” he added.
(That is why we are pushing for close coordination with the Department of Agriculture. Once we identify areas that will lack irrigation, we can plant various high-value crops there instead.)
Among the high-value crops he mentioned were corn and mung beans (munggo).
Guillen clarified that a lack of full irrigation does not mean fields must remain unplanted, emphasizing the critical role of interagency coordination.

NIA also urged collaboration with other government agencies, including the Department of Labor and Employment and the Department of Social Welfare and Development, to provide additional intervention measures once El Niño hits.
Farming along irrigation canals
NIA assured the public that irrigation shortages will not cause food prices to increase.
The agency highlighted its program promoting vegetable planting along irrigation canals.

“Pagkahaba-haba po ng ilang, daang libong kilometro po ang ating irrigation sa buong Pilipinas, eh kung magsipag lang yung ating mga farmers, yung ating mga irrigators association at magtanim po sa mga gilid ng irrigation natin ay malaking bagay po yan,” Guillen said.

(We have hundreds of thousands of kilometers of irrigation canals across the Philippines. If our farmers and irrigators' associations actively plant along the banks of these canals, it will be a huge help.)
Guillen said that from 2023 to 2025, vegetable farming along irrigation canals generated P1.6 billion in extra income for farmers nationwide. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: Chel Diokno: Prosecution to respect court's voting threshold decision
articles.summary: The prosecution team will respect whatever decision the Senate impeachment court makes on the voting threshold needed to either convict or acquit Vice President Sara Duterte in her impeachment trial,…

blocks.text: SARA DUTERTE IMPEACHMENT TRIAL
Published September 20, 2026 5:16pm

The prosecution team will respect whatever decision the Senate impeachment court makes on the voting threshold needed to either convict or acquit Vice President Sara Duterte in her impeachment trial, Akbayan Party-list Representative Chel Diokno said on Sunday.
“We believe that this matter is truly in the hands of the Senate as the impeachment court. Whatever decision they make on this issue, we will respect it,” Diokno told Super Radyo dzBB.
Diokno said the prosecution team is not focused on the number of votes needed for conviction but on presenting solid evidence before the impeachment court to secure Duterte’s conviction.

“We are not focused on the issue of the voting threshold. Our focus is on presenting the strongest possible case. Whatever decision the Senate impeachment court makes, we will abide by it,” Diokno said.
Oral arguments between the prosecution and defense teams are scheduled for Tuesday, September 23, 2026, in relation to the 16-vote threshold currently set for Duterte’s conviction.
In a separate dzBB interview, Senator JV Ejercito said he hoped senator-judges would be given time to study the arguments and inputs presented on the voting threshold.
“I'm asking for a few days, if possible, to absorb and study it,” he said.

Earlier this week, senator-judges sought the insights of former Supreme Court justices on whether senators who are detained, in hiding or abroad should be included in the voting on whether to convict or acquit Duterte.
Three of the four legal experts said the Senate impeachment court could change the 16-vote threshold for conviction, arguing that the Senate has the authority to try and decide impeachment cases.

Currently, Senators Jinggoy Estrada and Rodante Marcoleta are detained over separate plunder charges, while Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa is in hiding amid an arrest warrant issued by the International Criminal Court. Senator Loren Legarda, meanwhile, has been absent for weeks due to health concerns and is currently abroad.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Ukraine fires more than 1,000 drones at Russia, including hundreds launched at Moscow
articles.summary: Across the wider Moscow region, the attack killed two people and wounded 20, local Gov. Andrei Vorobyov said. The dead were a 74-year-old man and a 44-year-old woman, he said.

image.caption: An apartment building damaged in what authorities described as a Ukrainian drone strike, amid the Russia-Ukraine conflict in Sofyino settlement in the Ramensky district of the Moscow region on Sunday. (Reuters)

blocks.text: World
Across the wider Moscow region, the attack killed two people and wounded 20, local Gov. Andrei Vorobyov said. The dead were a 74-year-old man and a 44-year-old woman, he said.
Moscow's mayor described wave of drones as 'largest ever' attack on Russian capital

Ukrainian forces fired more than 1,000 drones at Russia overnight, including hundreds launched toward Moscow, officials said Sunday as the Kremlin was wrapping up the third and last day of its parliamentary elections.
Moscow's mayor described the wave of drones as the "largest ever" attack on the Russian capital and said there had been damage to a Moscow oil refinery and a residential building.
There was no immediate comment from Ukraine on the attack.

The voting in Russia was the country's first wartime parliamentary election — a balloting that was virtually devoid of opposition to President Vladimir Putin's policies and is all but certain to cement the Kremlin's dominance.
One of Russia's deadly jet-powered drones crashed in this backyard

Russia also held voting in four Ukrainian regions that Moscow illegally annexed after the war began but still doesn't fully control, and in Crimea, the Black Sea peninsula that was illegally annexed by Russia in 2014. Kyiv has denounced the action as illegal.
Russia's Ministry of Defence said that its forces shot down 1,100 Ukrainian drones across the country, as well as over the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the waters of the Black Sea.

items: Russian drones are stalking Ukrainian trains and trying to hobble the country's rail system

blocks.text: Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said that 450 drones had been destroyed en route to the Russian capital, and that the attack had damaged the Moscow Refinery and a residential building.
He said the "unprecedented attack" on the capital was an attempt to disrupt the elections.
"The enemy failed in this regard," he said.

articles.title: N.S. gave Saint Mary's University $25M to transform health care. Then it quietly killed the program
articles.summary: The Nova Scotia government gave Saint Mary's University $25 million in 2023 to create health-care data analytics and management programs to revolutionize the province's health-care system. Less than…

image.caption: Saint Mary's University received the $25 million in funding in 2023 after making a proposal — which was less than a page long — that it said would align with the province's plan for fixing the health-care system. (CBC)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia

The Nova Scotia government gave Saint Mary's University $25 million in 2023 to create health-care data analytics and management programs to revolutionize the province's health-care system. Less than three years after a high-profile announcement was made, the province quietly shut down the initiative.
Saint Mary's has 'not been able to demonstrate a concrete plan and adequate progress,' province says

It was March 2023 when Nova Scotia's then-advanced education minister appeared at Saint Mary's University, announcing $25 million in funding for the university to revolutionize the province's health-care system.
The money was intended to create health-care data analytics and management programs at the Halifax school, but Brian Wong offered few details on how that funding would lead to better health care.
"We need to come into the modern era as far as data and health care," Wong said at the time. "We've done it in other sectors many years ago, and it's time that we do it."
Over the last few years, Saint Mary's created and launched professional development courses, certificates in leadership, management and data analytics, and a master's in applied health sciences.

While those programs remain active, provincial officials viewed progress as slow and unsatisfactory, according to documents obtained through freedom of information requests to the university and the province.
Less than three years after the funding announcement, the province quietly decided early this year that the remaining $11 million of unused funding would not be used to continue the initiative.
Why the province shut the initiative down

A government document points to two primary reasons — the province's own fiscal constraints and "the fact that [Saint Mary's has] not been able to demonstrate a concrete plan and adequate progress against that plan."
Questions about whether the funding was a good use of public money emerged from the start.
The $25-million grant originated from a university pitch less than a page long that began by highlighting SMU's financial troubles, CBC News revealed in 2024.

items: Opposition questions how 1-page proposal earned Halifax university $25M from province

blocks.text: Unlike nearby rival Dalhousie University, Saint Mary's does not have a school of medicine or nursing.
In 2024, Wong defended the initiative.

"I'm not focused on a proposal," he said. "I'm really focused on what an outcome will be. And I know that they're working on it. And I'm confident that this will be an important program that will help direct health-care initiatives going forward."
The province has since changed course.

"It's the department's role to ensure appropriate oversight and accountability over public funding flowing to our post-secondary institutions. This is an example of where that oversight determined a need to change course," a government document notes.
What the university promised
In its pitch for the funding, Saint Mary's committed to several key initiatives, including:

items: Developing and offering health-care analytics programming to help workers make data-informed decisions.
Developing business administration, management and leadership courses for health-care administrators, staff, office directors, family doctors and practitioners.
Expanding articulation agreements to give Nova Scotia Community College (NSCC) health-care students more options to pursue degrees at Saint Mary's.

blocks.text: 'Unsatisfactory'
In provincial evaluations tracking these goals, the word "unsatisfactory" appears eight times on one page of the heavily-redacted documents.

"All three of the plans and their progress reports have been found to be unsatisfactory mainly due to the fact that there is still no plan in place to complete the initiative, spend the entirety of the $25M, and progress has been slow overall," a government document states.

items: 'This is going sideways fast': How Dalhousie scrapped a program's 63% tuition hike
Inside a Halifax university's battle to save face after spending nearly $500K on a football game

blocks.text: Focusing specially on the plan to have new articulation agreements with NSCC, the document states the Department of Advanced Education "does not see any value" in continuing to pursue this.

"Given SMU does not offer health education, there is limited if any opportunities for 2+2 offerings with the NSCC," it said. "The only real opportunity that may exist is with Health Information Management."
What SMU is saying
Saint Mary's stands by the initiative.

In a statement, Margaret Murphy, the university's associate vice-president of external affairs, said the university worked collaboratively with government and sector partners to support health-sector workforce development in the province.

"While the Province ultimately concluded that the initiative would not continue in its original form, the university believes important groundwork, program development and partnership activities were undertaken during the period of the agreement," she wrote.
"Saint Mary's remains committed to supporting workforce development and responding to the evolving needs of the province through its teaching, research and community partnerships."
Saint Mary's, like many Nova Scotia universities, faces financial strain driven by declining international enrolment and stagnant provincial operating grants.

items: Most of Nova Scotia's universities are in the red. Here's why, and what's next
2 N.S. universities say international student permit changes will cost them millions

blocks.text: But the way the deal between the province and Saint Mary's was structured indirectly helped the university with its financial woes.

Saint Mary's received the $25 million upfront and had to place the money in an externally restricted fund, separating it from general revenues so it could only be spent on the designated health-care programs.

However, the unused money was placed in an interest-bearing account, and that interest could be used for other expenses. Murphy confirmed the interest over the life of the initiative worked out to about $3.5 million and was used for student financial aid.

By early this year, roughly $11 million remained unspent. Around budget time, the province proposed allowing Saint Mary's to keep the unspent funds on the condition that this year's operating grant be reduced by an equivalent amount — a deal the university accepted.
"While some work has been completed, SMU has been unable to provide a satisfactory plan to the department for the remaining unspent funding," a government document notes.

articles.title: Chel Diokno: Higher penalties should be imposed on irresponsible gun owners
articles.summary: Higher penalties should be imposed to irresponsible gun owners who are found negligent in storing their firearms, Akbayan Party-list Representative Chel Diokno said Sunday.

blocks.text: Published September 20, 2026 4:59pm
Higher penalties should be imposed to irresponsible gun owners who are found negligent in storing their firearms, Akbayan Party-list Representative Chel Diokno said Sunday.
"Dapat rin bigyan rin ng mas malaking parusa ang mga gun owner kung sila ay pabaya," Diokno told Super Radyo dzBB.
(Gun owners should have heavier penalties if they are found to be negligent in storing their firearms.)
Diokno made the statement following a deadly school shooting in Banga, South Cotabato on Friday, where three students were killed and eight others were wounded.
The lawmaker said firing ranges should also be meted stricter penalties if these are found to allow children to handle firearms and teach them to shoot.

"Dapat mas mahigpit ang parusa dun sa mga firing range na pumapayag humawak ang bata ng baril at tinturuan kung paano bumaril, and that is also a factor na pwede ma-inflict na may hawak ng baril," Dikono said.

(There should be stricter penalties for firing ranges that allow children to handle firearms and teach them how to shoot, as these can also be factors that may lead to situations where a child has access to and being armed with a gun.)
Banga Mayor Albert Palencia reported that the weapon used in the incident belonged to the student's father, who is an employee of the Department of Education (DepEd).
Diokno said even without a law, the executive department can audit the firearms owned by all public officials and employees and require them to be inspected.

"Puede gawin ng Executive Department, mag utos sila ng isang audit ng lahat ng mga public official na may baril at alamin din nila yung safety steps na sinasagawa ng opisyal that is within their authority," Diokno said.

(The Executive Department can order an audit of all public officials who own or carry firearms and also review the safety measures being practiced by these officials, as this is within their authority.)
For private individuals, Diokno suggested that once a firearm is registered, owners should be required to agree to inspections on storing their firearms.
"Owning a gun is a big responsibility and there must be very stiff penalties for those who are negligent in terms of gun safety," Diokno said.
The lawmaker called on to strengthen the country's Anti-Bullying Law, as shooting incidents in schools have been rampant.
"Mayroon pang mas malalim na mga isyu na dapat tugunan at tingnan ang pamahalaan. Mukhang may koneksyon itong mga pangyayari sa bullying," Diokno said.
(We have more concerning issues we need to address. It seems that this has a connection with bullying.)

DepEd earlier said it would seek the help of the Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) and the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) to investigate the “true crime community” aspect following reports that the Banga National High School shooter was involved in it.
The student shooter was reportedly part of a “true crimes community" which may have led him to copy other shooting incidents, according to Banga Mayor Albert Palencia on Friday.
DILG Secretary Jonvic Remulla on Saturday said the shooter was into the deep dark web which influenced him. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: Russia: Ukrainian drone strike on Moscow kills 2
articles.summary: An oil refinery was hit in one of the largest attacks so far on the Russian capital, as the country holds a parliamentary election. Meanwhile, at least four people were killed in Russian strikes in…

image.caption: Smoke was seen rising from a refinery near MoscowImage: REUTERS

blocks.text: Two people were killed in a Ukrainian drone attack on the Moscow region, local authorities said Sunday, with an oil refinery in the region also being hit.
Energy infrastructure has been repeatedly targeted by both Ukraine and Russia, despite US President Donald Trump saying both sides had agreed to stop.
Ukraine's repeated targeting of oil refineries has led to oil product shortages and fuel price increases in Russia.
Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the strike had "a very significant impact," saying the oil in the hit refinery funds "billions of dollars to sustain the war machine."
"Moscow must end its brutal war and choose peace instead of building layered rings of air defense at the expense of other regions," Zelenskyy posted on X.

According to Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin, more than 1,600 drones have been intercepted by Russia since Saturday, including 450 aimed at the Russian capital, making it one the largest Ukrainian drone attacks on the city since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.
Moscow mayor accuses Ukraine of trying to disrupt parliamentary election
Sobyanin said that numerous drones had made it to the oil refinery, and another one hit an apartment. The scale of the damage done to the refinery has not been confirmed.
This comes as Russia is entering the last day of its three-day parliamentary election.
Sobyanin said the "unprecedented attack was clearly planned with the aim of disrupting the elections."
Meanwhile, in the eastern Ukrainian, Russian-occupied region of Kherson, a drone attack on a bus had killed two people, including an election official, Russian state news agency RIA reported.
War anxiety casts shadow over Russia's election
Three children killed in Kyiv region
In Ukraine, four people were killed in a Russian drone attack in the Kyiv region, local authorities said.
Among the casualties are a mother and her two 3-year-old children, as well as a girl who was taken to hospital in another district and later died.
The southwestern Fastiv district suffered damage to homes and industrial buildings.
Russia has been repeatedly carrying out drone attacks on the Ukrainian capital in recent weeks.

articles.title: ‘Terribly sorry’: Wrong Korean anthem played in Asian Games hockey
articles.summary: Lined up before their match in Asian Games men's hockey, South Korean players look around in confusion as the North Korean national anthem rings out at the stadium

blocks.text: REPRESENT. Athletes of South Korea in the athletes' parade during the opening ceremony of the 2026 Asian Games at the Paloma Mizuho Stadium in Nagoya, Japan.
Eloisa Lopez/REUTERS
Lined up before their match in Asian Games men's hockey, South Korean players look around in confusion as the North Korean national anthem rings out at the stadium

NAGOYA, Japan – The South Korean men’s hockey team was left bemused before its Asian Games match against Bangladesh on Friday, September 18, when North Korea’s national anthem was played instead of its own.
Lined up before the match, the South Korean players looked around in confusion as the anthem rang out at Green Stadium in Gifu, Japan.
The stadium announcer was quick to apologize for the mistake.
“We are really sorry, terribly sorry. National anthem for the Republic of Korea, we played a different song,” he said.
“I’m really sorry.”
South Korea won the match, 5-0.
The North Korean national anthem is banned in South Korea along with other symbols of its wartime foes.
The 1950-1953 Korean War ended in an armistice rather than a peace treaty, meaning the North and South are still technically at war.
The Asian Games organizing committee did not provide immediate comment on the anthem mix-up.

South Korea has complained of a number of organizational problems at the Games, with basketball players unhappy with the size of their rooms and transport issues disrupting preparations for the men’s football team, the defending champions. – Rappler.com
