A Russian cultural center in Berlin and the Russian consulate in Bonn were closed, which the German government said were being used as espionage centers. Moscow responded by closing the Goethe Institutes and the German consulate in St. Petersburg.

Putin has denied Russian responsibility for the Leipzig incident, calling it a "serious mistake" to blame Moscow, while Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov even described the accusations as the "beginning of a real war." But Baumann says: "We shouldn't give in to the fears being stoked, because they are part of Russia's strategy to weaken Germany and Europe."
AfD wants to resume relations with Russia

The German government is also facing domestic pressure as the far-right Alternative for Germany(AfD) has made gains in regional elections and is rising in the national polls. The AfD would prefer to end support for Ukraine and normalize relations with Russia, including deals on oil and gas. High fuel prices in Germany have only made the issue more explosive.

"German support for Ukraine worries many people," said Sven Leunig, political scientist at the University of Jena in Thuringia, following the election in the neighboring state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD won the September 6 election by a landslide. However, he noted, "it is less a fundamental rejection of the support itself than a reaction born of fear. People want to 'stay out' of the conflict so as not to be drawn into it more deeply themselves."

In the latest ARD Deutschlandtrend survey, 42% of respondents believe military aid to Ukraine has gone too far. "If public support weakens over the long term, the government will eventually have to respond," says Leunig.
Carry on or change course?

So far, the German government is sticking to its course, as Merz made clear once again following the AfD's election victory. But opinions on how to deal with Russia and the war in Ukraine differ not only among politicians but also among political scientists and experts.

Johannes Varwick of Halle University in Saxony-Anhalt believes it is long past time for a change of course: "German and European policy toward Ukraine resembles a mix of platitudes and wishful thinking," Varwick told DW. "It is high time for a course correction, and Germany should exert pressure on Ukraine to move closer to the latest American proposals, which aim for a compromise and could thus possibly bring about a political solution."

Baumann, on the other hand, argues: "Supporting Ukraine remains the best investment for safeguarding German and European interests. The government has recognized this and should stick to this course and continue to communicate it as such." However, it is important that Berlin act in concert with its European partners.

The war in Ukraine has now lasted longer than World War I. And there is no end in sight. Hopes that Russian-German relations will return to the way they used to be seem illusory for the foreseeable future.
This article was translated from German.

articles.title: Ukraine steps up measures to protect railways
articles.summary: As Russia increases its attacks on Ukraine's rail infrastructure, the Ukrainian government has called for help to replace destroyed locomotives and is making plans to keep passengers safe.

image.caption: Ukrainian trains are increasingly the target of Russian drones Image: Ukrainian State Emergency Service/AFP

blocks.text: Recent months have seen a rise in Russian drone attacks on locomotives, stations, and infrastructure. More than 1,600 attacks were reported in the first eight months of 2026, according to Oleh Holovashchenko from Ukrzaliznytsia, the state rail operator.

On September 16, a train traveling between the capital Kyiv and Mykolaiv in southern Ukraine was struck by a Russian drone. The day before, another train in the Volhynia region was attacked near the Polish border.

Two days earlier, a drone had struck the locomotive of a passenger train at the Yahodyn border crossing, just two kilometers (1.2 miles) from Polish territory. Nobody was injured, as Ukrzaliznytsia's monitoring system had previously detected the drone and the train had been evacuated about 15 minutes before the attack. At the time, CIA Director David Petraeus was on another train at the same station.

A separate train carrying several former European leaders, including ex-British Prime Minister Boris Johnson and security advisers had stopped at the station earlier the same day. The Ukrainian authorities believe that this diplomatic train was the drone's actual target, but the train departed earlier than scheduled.
'Putin's terror' against Ukrainian logistics

Russia has damaged or destroyed more than 500 Ukrainian locomotives since its full-scale invasion of Ukrainebegan in 2022. More than half of these attacks happened this year, according to a post on the social media platform X by Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha. He said that part of "Putin's terror" was to destabilize Ukraine's logistics system.

The minister called on international partners to tighten sanctions against Russia further and to provide financial assistance to the Ukrainian government so that it can procure more locomotives that are compatible with Ukraine's Soviet-era broad-gauge (1,520 millimeters or almost 5 feet).

"Ukraine's railway keeps the country moving," Sybiha said. "It enables the rapid evacuation of civilians from frontline areas, transports essential cargo, and keeps grain and other critical goods moving across the country."

Russia was specifically targeting locomotives because they were ideal from a technical point of view, said Vasyl Shevchenko, a former Ukrainian deputy transport minister. "A locomotive's thermal signature is very large, and almost impossible to miss," he told DW. "The impact of a strike can be devastating, because 50 kilograms (110 pounds) of explosives in a diesel locomotive can cause several metric tons of fuel to detonate and completely destroy it. A strike on an electric locomotive will cause a fire that can paralyze an entire stretch of track. That's why they are targeting areas where the loss of a single train can bring traffic to a standstill."

Shevchenko also pointed out that locomotives could not be replaced immediately but had to be ordered in advance and this could take years. Ukrzaliznytsia says that negotiations are underway with various international partners and a contract has already been signed with the French company Alstom. These locomotives are scheduled to start arriving next year.

In the meantime, trains are also being repaired. "While our top priorities used to be saving on costs, providing comfort to the train crew and making sure the trains were attractive, these have changed," Holovashchenko said. "What is most important today is that the locomotive is technically sound and ready to transport passengers and freight." But he added that it was difficult to protect trains against Russia's weapons.

blocks.caption: Ukrainian authorities are trying to ensure trains are evacuated before a drone strikes Image: Valentyn Ogirenko/REUTERS

blocks.text: Zelenskyy intensifies protection of critical infrastructure

On September 15, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy held a meeting of the staff of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief to discuss strengthening the protection of critical infrastructure and logistics.

The key issues were contracts for the production of protection systems for critical infrastructure and logistics, but he added that there were plans to expand the electronic warfare component and reorganize the operation of designated mobile fire teams, as well as strengthening air defense lines.

Zelenskyy said that decisions on backup logistics routes in frontline regions were also being made, and he had instructed Ukraine's Finance Ministry of to find additional funding for the logistics sector.

blocks.caption: Experts say it is technically very easy to target a locomotive Image: Odesa Regional Military Administration/AFP

blocks.text: Ukrzaliznytsia sets up monitoring centers

According to Holovashchenko, Ukrzaliznytsia is also seeking its own answers to the new challenges and there are plans to develop early detection systems. He said that a monitoring center had been established to track the movement of drones and trains all over Ukraine.

The fact that Russia has started to use jet-powered Shahed-type drones, which are much faster than previous models, has made it more difficult and given less time to respond. "We used to wait longer to stop trains so we could evacuate passengers," Holovashchenko said. "Now, there are more precautionary stops. But in general, we try not to go into areas where there is a potential danger."

Buses are deployed in areas of particularly high risk and the "train plus bus" concept is being expanded in cooperation with military authorities. Passengers are also being given instructions on how to respond in the event of an alarm and advised to try to get further away from a station than previously.

The most difficult question remains where they should be evacuated to. Holovashchenko said that the monitoring centers had access to maps showing all the shelters along train routes and that dispatchers always tried to stop trains near them, but this was not always possible. He said that train personnel were receiving special psychological support to help passengers.

Ukrzaliznytsia is currently preparing for winter, while working with foundations and other donors to ensure that trains will be heated. Evacuations will be even more difficult as temperatures drop. "This is no easy task. We're providing blankets, rain jackets, and equipment so that train staff can supply passengers with at least the bare necessities if their train comes to a standstill in the middle of nowhere because of a snowstorm, Holovashchenko said.
This article was originally published in Ukrainian.
Ukraine's unbreakable line: Trains to the frontline

articles.title: CNN, MS NOW and Politico denied access to White House
articles.summary: Three US news outlets said their journalists were blocked from entering the White House grounds, hours after President Donald Trump announced bans on several media outlets.

image.caption: CNN Senior White House Reporter Betsy Klein was denied entry to the White House on SaturdayImage: Jose Luis Magana/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: News outlets CNN, MS NOW and Politico on Saturday signaled they would take legal action after their journalists were denied access to the White House grounds earlier in the day.
It comes a day after US President Donald Trump announced he would ban the three news outlets from 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue in a row over their coverage of his presidency.
Trump has accused the media of "fake news" over their often critical coverage of his second term in office.
Experts say the bans conflict with the United States Constitution's First Amendment protections for free speech and press freedom.
Trump bans media outlets from White House
What did CNN, MS NOW and Politico say?
CNN reported that its journalist Betsy Klein was denied access at the White House on Saturday morning and her press pass was seized.

"CNN’s mission to report on the U.S. government will continue regardless of any attempts to restrict physical access to the White House and other government buildings, or any other attempts to impede our journalism,” a statement from the channel said.
“We have a right under the U.S. Constitution to do our reporting without hindrance or interference from the government and this ban is an illegal assault on this fundamental right."

blocks.caption: MS NOW White House reporter Akayla Gardner broadcast from outside the White House after she was denied entry on SaturdayImage: Jose Luis Magana/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Meanwhile, the left-leaning MS NOW, whose journalists were also turned away from the White House grounds on Saturday, said in a statement that it would challenge Trump's ban.

"The White House belongs to the American people and the decisions made inside are funded by our tax dollars,” the network said. "MS NOW intends to take any and all steps necessary to defend our First Amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy.”

Politico's global editor-in-chief Jonathan Greenberger, meanwhile, wrote in an email to staff: “A few minutes ago, our colleague Cheyenne Haslett attempted to enter the White House to do her job as a POLITICO reporter."
"Secret Service denied her entry to the complex and confiscated the pass that allows her access to the White House.
"We stand by her and all reporters here covering the White House. As we said yesterday, we will vigorously defend our First Amendment rights,” Greenberger wrote.

blocks.caption: Politico White House reporter Cheyenne Haslett was also denied entry to the White House a day after Trump's announcementImage: Jose Luis Magana/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: What did Trump accuse US media outlets of?
In a post on his Truth Social network, Trump said the media outlets "shouldn't be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they're covering the president of the United States."
"Other fake news media outlets to follow," he warned.
Trump said there was no one incident that prompted the ban, telling reporters in the Oval Office, "It's really just cumulative stories over the past few years."
"I don't have to let them into my, into the people's house," he added.

blocks.caption: Trump's relationship with the media is often punitiveImage: Alex Brandon/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: It was unclear whether the banned media outlets would also be blocked from flights aboard the presidential plane, Air Force One.
The US is just weeks away from the November 3 midterm elections in which Trump's Republican Party will struggle to defend narrow majorities in Congress.
With the president's approval ratings at 35%, near historic lows, Reuters/Ipsos polls also show Democrats ahead by around 7-9 points.
Trump's war with the press
During his second term, Trump has continued to round on journalists he deems critical to his administration — a tactic he employed when first elected in 2016.
Last year, he banned the Associated Press news agency from the usual pool of journalists that report on the presidency over its refusal to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America.
He has, however, given closer access to new, far-right media outlets seen as more sympathetic to his policies.
Trumps say comedian Jimmy Kimmel should be fired
Trump has even called on the US media regulator to remove the licenses of several broadcasters, whose comedy or news shows have mocked his policies and family.
The president has also filed several lawsuits against the Wall Street Journal, the New York Times, the BBC and Iowa's Des Moines Register, sometimes costing the media outlets millions in settlements.

articles.title: Journalists denied White House access after Trump banned some media outlets
articles.summary: CNN, MS NOW and Politico reporters' White House press badges were confiscated, the outlets reported.

blocks.text: "The officer asked me to hand over my badge. He said that it was disabled," MS NOW reporter Akayla Gardner said. "I asked why I was not able to get inside. He said it was above him."

Gardner added that while her and her colleague's badges were disabled, an MS NOW producer was still able to scan her badge to get in, though she was not given an explanation as to why the producer's badge still worked.
CNN reporter Betsy Klein said a Secret Service agent told her her badge had been deactivated.
Later on Saturday morning, Politico said its reporter Cheyenne Haslett was denied entry and Secret Service revoked her pass.
All three outlets have spoken out against the decision, accusing Trump of violating their constitutional rights to free speech and freedom of the press.
An MS NOW spokesperson said in a statement that the White House "belongs to the American people and the decisions made inside are funded by our tax dollars".
MS NOW said it "intends to take any and all steps necessary to defend our First Amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy".

Politico Editor-in-Chief Jonathan Greenberger said in an internal email, shared in the outlet's Playbook newsletter, that the company stands by its reporters and will "vigorously defend" their First Amendment rights.
And CNN said, "We have a right under the US Constitution to do our reporting without hindrance or interference from the government and this ban is an illegal assault on this fundamental right."
In his announcement, Trump did not mention specific stories or reporting from the three outlets that prompted the move, but later said "it's really just cumulative stories over the last few years".

Trump added that there "may be others to join them", but has not given a directive banning additional news outlets. When later asked by a reporter what he meant by others to come, Trump responded: "Others to come in terms of fake news? Well, you know, the New York Times is fake news, the Washington Post is fake news."
Several groups dedicated to the freedom of the press have called out Trump's White House ban as illegal and unconstitutional.

A major group that provides legal services to the media - the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press - said it expected Trump's ban to be struck down quickly by the courts because it was "flatly unconstitutional".

"The First Amendment is clear that once the White House invites in some journalists, it can't ban others because it doesn't like their reporting," said Bruce Brown, president of the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, which provides legal services to the media.

It's the latest in a series of moves by the administration to target media outlets Trump says are critical of him, including legal action against US and international outlets like The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, and the BBC.
Some of the lawsuits have resulted in media organisations agreeing to pay multimillion dollar settlements. Trump's lawsuit against the BBC is ongoing.
Additional reporting from Bernd Debusmann Jr and Max Matza.

articles.title: Thick smoke seen near Riyadh airport after air-raid alerts in Saudi capital
articles.summary:
Authorities also issued warnings for Jeddah and Yanbu, a major industrial port and home to vital oil facilities

Flames and a large plume of black smoke were seen rising above Riyadh airport…

blocks.text: Flames and a large plume of black smoke were seen rising above Riyadh airport in Saudi Arabia on Saturday after the government sent air-raid alerts to citizens by phone overnight warning of aerial attacks.

Explosions were heard in the capital and firefighters battled to extinguish the flames of a burning fuel tank emblazoned with the logo of the Saudi oil company Aramco near the city’s King Khalid international airport.
It is the first time the government has issued such alerts for Riyadh since fighting with the Iran-backed Houthis in neighbouring Yemen escalated in July.
Residents told Agence France-Presse that hours after the alert, they had heard what sounded like another round of explosions echoing through parts of the Saudi capital.
According to tracking website FlightRadar24, there are “major problems” at the airport and it has been listed under its maximum disruption index.
“In the direction of the airport, we saw black smoke and fire,” one resident told AFP, speaking on condition of anonymity.

The Saudi civil defence force sent air-raid alerts overnight on Friday to residents of Riyadh, Jeddah and other cities including Yanbu, a major industrial port which is home to critical oil facilities.
The all-clear was given shortly afterwards, but residents were encouraged not to gather in crowds.

The UN security council condemned the continued ​Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia in a statement on Friday. It said they had included attacks that affected civilian and energy infrastructure and had injured civilians, including women and children.
It also condemned the Houthis’ military offensive in Yemen, where nearly 105,000 people have fled their homes, the International Organization for Migration said on Wednesday.

The security council’s 15 members called for “practical cooperation” to prevent the Houthis from acquiring arms, military training, financing and other military-related assistance needed to carry out their attacks. They stressed that all countries must enforce the UN arms embargo against the group.

The Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group had foiled unspecified “criminal attempts” ⁠in the Yemeni capital of Sana’a, blaming Saudi Arabia and vowing a response. The group also says the Saudi air force has conducted hundreds of airstrikes against it in recent days.

The Houthis recently seized control of strategic the Red Sea islands of Greater and Lesser Hanish. Earlier this month, the group captured the port of Mokha and Perim island in the Bab al-Mandab strait, fueling fears the world could face a second oil supply crisis.

articles.title: Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania: Will economy shape the vote?
articles.summary: Voters in the eastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania head to the polls on Sunday, with the Social Democrats and far-right AfD neck and neck. Here's a look at key economic issues that could…

image.caption: Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania is Germany's second-most popular vacation destinationImage: Jens Büttner/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The recent election victory of the far-right AfD party in Saxony-Anhalt has shaken up Germany's political landscape. Although Saxony-Anhalt is only a small state, the AfD's landslide win with nearly 44% of the vote has drawn considerable international attention, as it means this would the first time that a far-right party will likely enter a German government since World War II.

That is not expected to happen in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, where voters head to the ballot box on Sunday. State Premier Manuela Schwesig of the center-left Social Democrats remains popular, as polls show, though she isn't without her critics.

The latest polls suggest a neck-and-neck race between the Social Democrats and AfD, rather than a landslide victory for any one party. In fact, the Social Democrats' approval ratings have been on the rise and could indicate a successful final push, potentially returning Schwesig to power.
Lower wages, but solid economic growth

Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, like Saxony-Anhalt, is in eastern Germany, but its economy is relatively stable, even though unemployment stands at 7.8%, slightly above the national average, and the median gross annual salary is €47,750 ($54,800) — about €6,000 less than the German average. But Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania has seen solid economic growth in recent years.

Jochen Schulte, state secretary in the state's Economy Ministry, said Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania's economy has expanded by 5% in inflation-adjusted terms since 2020, compared with 4.6% for Germany overall.

Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania has a large agricultural sector, although it employs relatively few people. Back when the state was part of East Germany, farms were consolidated into large, state-run enterprises known as agricultural production cooperatives, rather than privately organized as in West Germany.

blocks.caption: Farms in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, once consolidated into large, state-run cooperatives, are still bigger than the German averageImage: Jens Büttner/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: In many instances, these farm sizes have remained the same since reunification. A typical agricultural company in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania will control about 280 to 283 hectares (up to 700 acres) of land, whereas the national average is only about 65 hectares.

The state's now private agricultural companies continue to benefit from their large size, ensuring efficient labor use, strong market positioning, greater market power through centralized purchasing, and a strong negotiating position when selling produce.
Many jobs in shipbuilding, tourism

The state's second major industry is shipbuilding and maritime services, which accounts for a significant share of economic output. Being on Germany's Baltic Sea coast, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania has also benefited from the recent investment boom in its defense sector. This has brought business — and jobs — to major shipyards in Wismar and Stralsund, at companies like Thyssenkrupp Marine Systems and other shipbuilders.
Hundreds of fake posts target German elections

Tourism is another key sector in the state. Until 1990, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania was one of the most important travel destinations for East Germans. Since the fall of the Berlin Wall, Germans from east and west have continued to flock to the Baltic coast, and the region is Germany's second-most popular vacation destination.

That said, relatively few people are directly employed in the tourism sector. That is in part merely a statistical quirk, as many tourism jobs overlapping with service jobs, and also because many tourism jobs are seasonal.

According to figures from the Economy Ministry and industry reports, some 150,000 to 160,000 jobs depend on tourism, either directly or indirectly. Water-based tourism, whether on lakes or the Baltic Sea coast, accounts for an estimated 19,000 jobs.
Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania has few large enterprises, such as automakers and chemical companies, which makes its state and civil service branch the region's largest employer.

Rostock-based AIDA Cruises is another major employer. So is Nordex SE, a manufacturer of wind turbines with production facilities in various regions. German rail operator Deutsche Bahn provides many jobs through its service and maintenance hubs, as do the major ports of Rostock and Sassnitz.
5 things you need to know about Nord Stream
Fossil fuels, renewables power regional economy
Another key industry is the energy sector, with large quantities of Germany's fossil fuels brought in via the Baltic Sea.

When imports of Russian gas came to a standstill in 2022 following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the Nord Stream gas pipeline connection points near Lubmin lost their significance. However, a large portion of Germany's liquefied natural gas imports are still unloaded, processed and distributed in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

blocks.caption: The coastal state has increasingly invested in renewable energy, including wind powerImage: Jens Büttner/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Energy availability, not only from fossil fuels such as oil and gas, but also from green sources such as wind and solar power, is becoming increasingly important for the state as well.
In August, the Schwarz Group — which operates the Lidl and Kaufland supermarket chains — announced it would invest €5.6 billion ($6.4 billion) in the construction of a data center south of Rostock.
During the project's presentation in the state capital, Schwerin, the company said its investments in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania could reach tens of billions of euros.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Converse pulls 'deeply upsetting' advert after backlash
articles.summary: Social media users say an image from the brand's Instagram account resembled a KKK hood and hanging.

blocks.text: American footwear brand Converse has pulled an advert that social media users said evoked Ku Klux Klan imagery, saying it recognised "that we got this wrong".
The photo, posted to the company's Instagram account, received backlash online after critics described lighting in the image as looking like a white pointed hood.
A pair of shoes, dangling in the picture, were also likened to an image of a lynching victim by social media users.

In an apology, first issued on Friday, Converse said the photo had been removed from its social media channels and it was working to remove it elsewhere. "This should not have happened and we will do better," it said.
The statement also said: "We're sorry. We understand why this image is deeply upsetting and recognize that we got this wrong".

articles.title: 'Enough is enough': Women protest after string of murders near Johannesburg
articles.summary: The police have since set up a task team to investigate the murders and have urged women in the Kempton Park area to avoid walking or running alone "particularly in isolated areas".

blocks.text: Runners gathered in South Africa to pay tribute to Elizabeth Moselakgomo after her body was found east of Johannesburg.
She is one of nine women found in the Kempton Park area, since July.
The jogger, known as "Tsontso", went missing during a routine run.
Runners organised an event in city of Centurion to honour her and defend women's right to run freely.
"This is for her - we just want to live and go running and come back home without having to think that it may be one of us", said Nonhle Mpohlo.
In Cape Town, people gathered in a vigil to honour the victims and called on the government to act.
The police have since set up a task team to investigate the murders and have urged women in the Kempton Park area to avoid walking or running alone "particularly in isolated areas".

articles.title: Long-standing Winnipeg hotel reconnects with 'piece of history' after nearly 120 years
articles.summary: The Northern Hotel on Winnipeg's Main Street has reconnected with a piece of its history, after an Alberta-based antiques dealer stumbled upon a custom cash register made for the business more than a…

image.caption: Keith Horn, owner of the Northern Hotel in Winnipeg, stands with an antique mechanical cash register made for the Main Street business in 1907. (Tyson Koschik/CBC)

blocks.text: Manitoba

The Northern Hotel on Winnipeg's Main Street has reconnected with a piece of its history, after an Alberta-based antiques dealer stumbled upon a custom cash register made for the business more than a century ago.
Antique mechanical cash register built in 1907 returns to Northern Hotel
A long-standing Winnipeg hotel has reconnected with a piece of its history, after an Alberta-based antiques dealer stumbled upon a cash register made for the business more than a century ago.
The register, built by National Cash Register Company in 1907, is engraved with the name of the Northern Hotel and was once a critical part of the Main Street establishment's daily operations.
"It's kind of neat. It's all mechanical — and the fact that it still works, a lot of it is just a testament to the craftsmanship that they did 120 years ago," said hotel owner Keith Horn.
"It's a piece of history."
Horn purchased the register in late July from Franz Giesen, co-owner of Frantic4tiques — an online business based in Mannville, Alta., east of Edmonton.
Giesen said he spotted the cash register for sale on Facebook Marketplace and made the nearly 1,200-kilometre drive from Mannville to Winnipeg to collect it.

"I thought on the way in, I'm like, how cool would it be if I was able to reconnect this cash register with the owner of the Northern Hotel? So then, when I got to the city, I made the phone call," Giesen said.
Horn said he was initially skeptical about buying the antique, but came around to the idea after learning more about it.
Giesen used a serial number stamped on the register to determine when it was built. He believes the machine, which is covered in embellishments, was cast in metal.
It weighs more than nine kilograms and still makes a satisfying ring when punching in the numbers, which range in value from five cents to $10.
"Just wondering what, back in 1907, was $10, when rooms back then [only cost] up to $2," Horn said, smiling.
"I guess they were very hopeful."
This particular model included specialty buttons that allowed the hotel to track how many meals or cigars it sold, and was capable of keeping a running total of the day's earnings.

While the exact history of the cash register is murky, but it's nearly as old as the hotel itself, which was built in 1906. Giesen learned the register wound up in the care of a former radio repair shop a short distance from the Northern Hotel sometime in the 1950s.
It was then inherited by the daughter of the radio shop owner, who kept it in her basement until he bought it from her, said Giesen.

items: New life being breathed into Winnipeg Hotel, oldest building in city's downtown

blocks.text: "Everything from back then is just out of this world, right? Things were made to last, nothing was made to be tossed away. There is a reason why these things still exist," he said.
Horn said he plans to clean the register, and then put it on display inside the Northern Hotel.
120-year-old piece of Winnipeg history comes home
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Tyler Searle covers news, events and issues affecting Manitoba's Interlake region for CBC. He previously worked as a general assignment reporter for the Winnipeg Free Press. He is based in Selkirk, and can be reached by email at tyler.searle@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Millions without power as Cuba hit by latest major blackout
articles.summary: Widespread power outages have become increasingly common due to fuel shortages made worse by a US blockade.

blocks.text: Millions in Cuba were left without power on Friday as the country was plunged into yet another major blackout.
The country's entire electricity grid suffered "total disconnection" that triggered a nationwide outage, Cuba's energy ministry said.
Power was restored to some priority areas by late evening, including those near hospitals and water pumping stations in the capital Havana, grid operator UNE said.

It is at least the sixth partial or total blackout to hit Cuba this year, where ageing electricity infrastructure and chronic fuel shortages have been placed under further strain by a US blockade on oil shipments to the communist-run nation.
UNE said the outage started just before 14:00 local time on Friday (18:00 GMT) due to a transmission fault coupled with poor weather conditions in central Cuba.
Protocols to begin the "gradual restoration" of power were activated, the operator's national load dispatch director Felix Estrada said, with the process ongoing on Saturday.
Cuba relies heavily on fuel imports, meaning tight US sanctions and an oil blockade since the start of the year have exacerbated existing shortages.
Food and medicine have also become more scarce, with hospitals struggling to function normally and schools and government offices having to close.
"Lately, it's becoming a habit," Havana resident Frank Lorenzo told news agency Reuters on Friday.
"Before it happened less frequently - once a month… just yesterday we were 24 hours without electricity, they turned it on for just an hour and it went down again."
"It's one thing after another: no water, no gas for cooking, no electricity," 36-year-old schoolteacher Lidia Fernandez told news agency AFP. "Honestly, I don't know how we haven't gone crazy."
Francisco Rodriguez, 78, said his home had already gone without power for 28 hours on Friday and feared he would not have light "for several days".
The repeated blackouts have prompted rare protests in Cuba, where unauthorised demonstrations are illegal and those who defy the ban risk being jailed.

Havana has blamed its fuel crisis on the Trump administration and denounced all of its sanctions - including a new round announced in August - which are part of a wider pressure campaign against the Caribbean island's leadership.

Cuba's regional ally Venezuela was believed to have sent it around 35,000 barrels of oil a day - about half of its oil needs - until Venezuela's own supplies were cut off following the US seizure of its President Nicolás Maduro in January.
US President Donald Trump has threatened tariffs on countries shipping oil to Havana, and a number of such shipments have been seized by the US.

Washington meanwhile attributes Cuba's energy crisis to poor internal management and has accused it of posing a "national security threat". Trump has openly discussed toppling its leadership, including threatening a "friendly takeover" in March this year.

articles.title: Oktoberfest 2026: Everything you need to know
articles.summary: This year, AI will be used to manage overcrowded situations. Find all the numbers surrounding the fest — including the price of water!

image.caption: Oktoberfest attracts millions of visitors every yearImage: Wolfgang Maria Weber/IMAGO

blocks.text: On Saturday, September 19, at noon, Oktoberfest will once again open with the ceremonial tapping of the keg, during which the mayor of Munich drives a tap into the first wooden barrel of beer and calls out "O'zapft is," a Bavarian phrase that translates to "It's tapped."
His call will be followed by 12 gunshots, a signal that lets all festival tents know that they can start serving beer.
More than 6 million people are expected at the world's largest Volksfest, which runs this year through October 4.
Oktoberfest: What to know about 'the best party in Germany'
Expanded security measures to prevent overcrowding
The festival grounds are enormous: Oktoberfest takes place on Munich's Theresienwiese, a 34.5-hectare site roughly the size of 48 soccer fields.
But crowds can swell, especially on weekends — sometimes to dangerous levels.
Last year, officials had to temporarily close the entrances.

One reason is that nearly all 38 beer tents operate in two or three reservation shifts. When one group of guests leaves and the next arrives at the 14 large tents — which each accommodate several thousand people — huge numbers of visitors end up trying to enter and exit at the same time.
That's how, on one Saturday afternoon at last year's Oktoberfest, the crowds became so dense that movement temporarily came to a standstill. The crush caused some visitors to panic.
To prevent that from happening again, the city of Munich has overhauled its security plan for this year's festival.
Twenty-six new cameras, in addition to 56 police cameras, will monitor the grounds, while an AI system will analyze visitor flows and issue alerts if areas become overcrowded.

blocks.caption: Around 300,000 people were at Oktoberfest simultaneously on the second Saturday of the festival in 2025Image: Frank Hoermann/SVEN SIMON/picture alliance

blocks.text: A newly established coordination center is also intended to improve communication between security agencies and event organizers.
Organizers and police have drawn up a plan to defend against drones over the grounds, though no details have been disclosed.
In addition, 600 police officers will be deployed on site.
Oktoberfest is famous worldwide, but most visitors are local
Oktoberfest may be known around the world as an international tourist attraction, but most of its visitors don't travel very far to get there.
A study commissioned by the city of Munich last year found that the festival remains overwhelmingly regional.

blocks.caption: Statistically speaking, two international guests sit at every 10-person table in the festival tentsImage: Maryam Majd/REUTERS

blocks.text: In 2025, 41% of visitors came from Munich, another 25% from the surrounding area and 9% from elsewhere in the region. In all, three-quarters of Oktoberfest's roughly 6.5 million visitors came from Bavaria. Another 4% came from elsewhere in Germany.

About 21% of visitors — roughly 1.35 million people — traveled from abroad. Americans made up the largest group of international visitors, accounting for just under 20% of the total, or more than 270,000 people. Italians were next, at just over 13%.
Beer prices rise again
Cannabis is banned throughout the festival grounds.

Alcohol, on the other hand, is available in whatever quantities visitors are willing — and able — to pay for. A Mass, the traditional 1-liter mug of beer served at Oktoberfest, costs between €14.80 and €15.90 ($17-$18.25) this year, only slightly more than last year.
A liter of table water comes in at a hefty €11, although the grounds also have several free drinking water fountains.
Visitors planning to enjoy one of Oktoberfest's many rides would be wise to stay relatively sober. Tickets cost anywhere from just under €5 to €14.

Germany's traditional fairground culture was officially added to the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2026, and that tradition remains very much alive at the 191st Oktoberfest. According to organizers, about 90% of the festival's more than 130 fairground operators can trace their roots back to the 19th century.
The festival remains decidedly traditional when it comes to payment, too: Many vendors still accept cash only. Visitors caught without any can withdraw money from ATMs on the grounds.
Dirndl or lederhosen for Oktoberfest?
Then there's the question of what to wear.
Bavarians who take pride in doing things properly generally show up in local traditional dress.

blocks.caption: Traditional garb can be seen at the annual breweries' paradeImage: Felix Hörhager/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The dirndl is the traditional dress worn by women and girls, which consists of close-fitting bodice with a low neckline, a blouse worn under the bodice, a wide high-waisted skirt and an apron.
Men wear lederhosen, the traditional leather shorts or knee-length breeches with suspenders.

For those who are not Bavarian, lederhosen and dirndls are certainly an option, but they're by no means required. Munich's event marketing department, Simply Munich, advises first-time visitors to consider renting traditional garb rather than buying it.

Be aware that locals find cheap imitations of traditional dress off-putting, as Simply Munich points out: "If you want to avoid wry looks, steer clear of Seppl hats, 'leather pants' made of cloth and garish mini plastic dirndls. With jeans and a checkered shirt, you'll definitely be more suitably dressed."
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Deadly shark attack prompts rare kill order in Western Australia
articles.summary: Police boats and helicopters are patrolling Perth's beaches as authorities continue their search for the swimmer's body, and the shark that attacked him.

blocks.text: A rare catch-and-kill order has been issued for a great white shark off the coast of Western Australia, after a man was killed while on a morning swim at a popular beach on Friday. His body has still not been found.
Authorities have said that beaches along the state's coast, including in the capital Perth, will remain closed until at least Sunday as the search for the shark continues.
It is the second shark attack in Western Australia (WA) this week, and the third fatal attack in the state this year.
The incident, at Sorrento Beach in Perth's north, has reignited debate about how to keep beachgoers safe in Australia.
The swimmer has been identified as 63-year-old Greg O'Neill, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC) has reported.
"Greg loved the ocean and was known as a passionate swimmer, sports lover, dedicated worker and an all-round generous, witty guy," his family said in a statement to the broadcaster.
Witness Jacqui Rapaic told the ABC that two men were swimming, but only one made it back to shore, and that she could see "a pool of blood" in the water.
Another witness told WAtoday that she saw the man being "mauled" as the shark "tossed him around like a fish".
Members of the public reported seeing a 2.5m-long (8ft 2in) shark at around the same time.
Authorities in Perth's Joondalup area, where Sorrento is located, said all beaches were closed "as a precautionary measure" and would remain so until at least midday on Sunday.
Pictures on Saturday showed the coastline being patrolled by a police boat and helicopter.
Catch-and-kill orders are rare and controversial in Australia, where great white sharks are a protected species.

WA Fisheries Minister Jackie Jarvis said that she took the "extraordinary step" of issuing the order after the shark was spotted by water police on Saturday morning, and "positively identified as the shark involved in the incident".
The minister said she authorised fisheries officers to "destroy the shark" if it could be captured because of the "exceptional circumstances" of the attack and the "hazard posed by the shark".
It is believed to be the first time in 10 years that such an order had been issued in WA, Jarvis added, emphasising that the order was not a widespread cull as the state has seen in the past.
The minister also said that the use of drones and tagging would be increased to help protect beachgoers.

Catching and killing sharks has a long and controversial history in Western Australia - there were months of huge protests in 2014 when the state government authorised a cull after a spate of attacks.

The incident in Sorrento is the second in WA this week - on Monday a 56-year-old man was bitten while surfing off the coast of Geraldton, 430km (270 miles) north of Perth. He survived but lost part of his leg, another surfer who rescued him told the ABC.
There have been five fatal shark attacks in Australia this year.

A 12-year-old boy died after he was bitten in Sydney Harbour in January, and three divers were fatally mauled in separate incidents between May and June - two in Western Australia and the third in Queensland.

articles.title: Rebels, workers, radicals: The making of 'Red Berlin'
articles.summary: Bloody May, student sit-ins and the squatter movement: Berlin has a long history as a hotbed for working-class organizing and radical left-wing politics.

image.caption: A Molotov cocktail explodes during the forced eviction of a squat in the Berlin district of Friedrichshain in 1990Image: Stefan Trappe/IMAGO

blocks.text: Berlin has a reputation for being unruly. When Jospeh Goebbels was appointed the Nazi Party's district leader in 1926, he described Berlin as "the reddest city in Europe besides Moscow." From the Tailors' Revolution of 1830 and the barricades of 1848, to the rise of a vast industrial working class later in the 19th century, revolution, protest and rebellion run deep throughout the city's history.

While the future German philosopher and revolutionary socialist Karl Marx was still in high school in the small town of Trier in Prussia's Rhine Province, Berlin was fast becoming a center of the country's labor movement. It was during the March Revolution of 1848 — a failed attempt to create a democratic German nation-state — that the General Workers' Brotherhood was founded, one of the first worker's organizations to become active in Germany.

blocks.caption: In March 1848, Berliners fought for basic freedoms and German unityImage: United Archives International/IMAGO

blocks.text: By the 1870s and 1880s, major industries from mechanical and railway engineering to ready-made clothing were located in the city. As the working-class population grew, this in turn impacted the city's political culture. "It became more populist in a positive sense: moving away from the traditional, elitist politics of the bourgeois liberals who had long dominated Berlin, and toward the inclusion of ordinary people, since at least men were now also important voters," Axel Weipert, a historian and author of the book "Red Berlin" (2019), tells DW.
Emergence of a radical labor movement

Berlin's labor movement became increasingly radical, partly in response to heavy-handed repression under the Chancellor Otto von Bismarck. Although Bismarck created the first modern welfare state to try and undercut the rising popularity of the socialist movement, he also introduced laws banning socialist and communist organizations, newspapers and public gatherings, as well as independent trade unions.

blocks.caption: A memorial to Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, who co-authored 'The Communist Manifesto' in 1848, still stands close to Berlin's city hallImage: Jürgen Ritter/IMAGO

blocks.text: After Bismarck resigned in 1890, the anti-socialist laws were repealed and the ideas of Karl Marx and his fellow revolutionary socialist Friedrich Engels became the ideology of what Weipert describes as a "genuine mass movement" in Berlin. The Social Democratic Party (SPD), Germany's oldest political party, was formed out of a merger between the General German Workers' Association and the social Democratic Workers' Party in 1875. Before World War I, the SPD was able to win far higher vote shares in Berlin than elsewhere in the country.

In 1914, the labor movement was seriously discredited when the SPD leadership and the trade unions decided not to oppose the war pushed by Kaiser Wilhelm II. But from 1916 onwards, Berlin became the center of mass labor strikes against the war. One of the earliest strikes was against the trial of anti-war socialist campaigner Karl Liebknecht. Together with Rosa Luxemburg and other left-wing radicals, Liebknecht founded the Spartacus League in Berlin, an underground group that later became the Communist Party of Germany (KPD).

blocks.caption: Karl Liebknecht (left) and Rosa Luxenburg were murdered by right-wing paramilitary soldiers of the Freikorps in BerlinImage: akg-images/picture-alliance

blocks.text: Triggered by war-weariness, severe food shortages and economic ruin, around half a million Berlin workers joined the January Strike of 1918. Supported by the Spartacus League, the anti-war strike was led by the Revolutionary Stewards, a clandestine network of factory workers and trade unions from large munitions and metal-working factories. The same group became a core organizing force behind the overthrow of the Kaiser in Berlin on November 9, 1918.
From left-wing unity to division

In the chaotic, war-torn city gripped by violent revolution, the Spartacist Uprising of 1919 was launched to overthrow Germany's provisional government and establish a republic of workers councils. Its violent suppression, which resulted in scores of deaths — Liebknecht and Luxemburg were both murdered by soldiers of right-wing paramilitary militias — permanently fractured the political left.

blocks.caption: Spartacist revolutionaries armed with machine guns aimed to establish a communist stateImage: Cola Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: As the capital of the newly founded Weimar Republic, Berlin remained a hotbed of radical politics in the interwar period. This was especially true in neighborhoods with large numbers of tenement buildings, such as Wedding, Kreuzberg and Neukölln, where thousands of factory workers lived in squalid conditions. The many large factories in Berlin also created shared interests and laid the groundwork for collective action.

"Bloody May" in 1929 saw brutal attacks on illegal May Day demonstrations which left at over 30 people dead. The SPD police president of Berlin had issued a ban on all public demonstrations for May Day, a ban defied by the KPD. In response, the police opened fire on protestors in the streets and also shot through windows in residential buildings, primarily in the working-class districts of Wedding and Neukölln.

blocks.caption: 'Bloody May' inspired the labor movement song 'Red Wedding' by Hanns Eisler and Erich WeinertImage: Atlantic Photo-Co/SVT/TT/IMAGO

blocks.text: During the Great Depression era, the SPD lost much of its support between 1929 and 1933, as joblessness ravaged the city. "Unemployment is critical — it meant that men were no longer attached to the SPD-led factory floor and trade union and the social bonds of these spaces and organizations," explains Pamela Swett, a historian at the University of Rhode Island. "Unmoored from the rhythm of daily life, men sought new bonds — new ways to feel self-respect and camaraderie with others." Some joined the KPD, which became known as the "Party of the Unemployed." Others joined far-right paramilitary groups such as the Nazi stormtroopers.
From student sit-ins to the housing crisis

After the Nazis took power in 1933, many of the labor movement leaders were killed or exiled. Then, in the aftermath of World War II, Berlin was divided into two separate political systems. East Berlin became the capital of the communist German Democratic Republic. Isolated from the Federal Republic of Germany, West Berlin deindustrialized, the labor movement weakened, and the SPD moved to the right.

During the Cold War, many left-leaning young men moved to West Berlin to evade military service. This intensified the student movement, the center of which was Berlin's Free University (Freie Universität). It was there, in leafy southwest Berlin, that historic sit-ins were held to protest the perceived authoritarianism of the government and the presence of former Nazi officials in positions of power. The fatal shooting of student Benno Ohnesorg by a police officer during a demonstration against the visiting Shah of Iran in 1967 radicalized a generation that led the widespread protests of 1968.

blocks.caption: The fatal shooting of student, Benno Ohnesorg, by police during protests against the Shah of Iran's visit in 1967 radicalized a generationImage: dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: In the early 1970s, a housing shortage led parts of the student movement but also apprentices and young migrant families to squat in West Berlin's empty buildings. "You have migrant laborers and young laborers participating, so this was part of working-class rebellion against capitalist housing," says Ralf Hoffrogge, a labor movement historian at Berlin's Free University.

Today, as gentrification sweeps the city, Berlin is home to the strongest and most radical tenants' movements in Germany. In a 2021 referendum, 59% of voters in the city approved the expropriation of property from private real-estate companies. Hoffrogge was part of the campaign, and his 2025 book "Loud Berlin" ("Das laute Berlin") explores how the housing crisis has become a catalyst for a "socialist renaissance" in the city. "It's not Berlin tenants against Berlin landlords, it's tenants against global capital. I think people have started to realize these contradictions and this is why class-based policy concepts are becoming popular again."

blocks.caption: 'Housing is not a commodity': Berlin's housing crisis and rapid gentrification have triggered new political initiatives in the cityImage: IPON/IMAGO

articles.title: India news: PM Modi says developing nations unfairly blamed for emissions
articles.summary: At the inauguration of a climate conference in New Delhi, PM Modi said developing countries are unfairly blamed for carbon emissions. An IIT Bombay professor has been accused of caste abuse. DW has…

image.caption: Prime Minister Narendra Modi and several other prominent leaders were present at the inauguration of the climate conferenceImage: ANI/IMAGO

blocks.text: September 20, 2026
Developing nations unfairly blamed for emissions, Modi tells climate conference
Prime Minister Narendra Modi has said developing countries are unfairly held responsible for carbon emissions despite their comparatively low per-capita output.
Modi made the remarks on Saturday as he inaugurated a two-day international conference on environmental and climate governance in New Delhi, organized by India's National Green Tribunal.

Speaking at the opening of the "Future of Environment and Climate Dynamics" conference at Vigyan Bhawan, Modi said, "We know that often the responsibility for carbon emissions is wrongly placed upon developing countries... the historical truth is that India's contribution per capita carbon emission is less than half of the global average."
"In developed countries, per capita carbon emissions are six times higher than in India."

He said India has consistently raised this point at global forums, including at the 2015 Paris climate summit, adding that India is the only G20 nation to have met its Paris commitments ahead of schedule.

The remarks come weeks after devastating floods hit India's northern neighbor, Nepal, killing over 1400 people. Nepal contributes roughly 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions, making it what the World Bank calls a "negligible contributor to climate change."

The conference, which ends Sunday, brings together judges and environmental officials from 17 countries as well as Indian Supreme Court and High Court judges, senior bureaucrats, and representatives of state environmental authorities, according to the Prime Minister's Office.

articles.title: Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania: SPD seeks to fend off AfD
articles.summary: For nearly three decades, the Social Democrats have governed Germany's northeastern state. If they can fend off the AfD, the result may boost the fortunes of the German government's junior coalition…

image.caption: Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania's state legislature is housed in Schwerin CastleImage: Jens Büttner/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Stretching along Germany's Baltic coast, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania is known for the tourist draws of Rügen and Usedom, the quiet island of Hiddensee with the grave of playwright Gerhart Hauptmann, and the historic universities of Greifswald and Rostock, among the oldest in the country. The state is also shaped by its industrial heritage, including its shipyards and the vast nuclear power plant at Lubmin, built in former East Germany and closed in 1995.

Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania is Germany's most sparsely populated federal state, with a population of just 1.57 million at the end of 2025. The unemployment rate in the structurally weak state stands at 8%, above the national average. At roughly 6%, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania also has by far the lowest share of foreign nationals of any of Germany's 16 federal states.

For many former East Germans, the state is associated with long summers spent at campsites and holiday resorts along the Baltic coast. It is also home to 16 national parks, more than any other federal state in Germany, and to the Mecklenburg Lake District, centered on Lake Müritz.

Yet this federal state was also the scene of some of the earliest violent attacks on asylum-seeker accommodations following German reunification. Images of burning housing blocks in Rostock-Lichtenhagen in August 1992 were broadcast around the world. That year, the number of asylum seekers in Germany reached a provisional peak of 440,000, fueling heated debates across the country.

In August of that year, hundreds of far-right rioters attacked a residential building in Rostock that housed around 100 people from Vietnam. The building was set on fire as some 3,000 local residents applauded the attackers. Miraculously, no one was killed, though many people were injured. It was the worst outbreak of racist violence in Germany since the Second World War.
Incumbency advantage may help Manuela Schwesig

Former Chancellor Angela Merkel had her electoral district in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. For around 28 years, the state has been governed by the Social Democratic Party (SPD) in coalition with various partners.

Most recently, it has been led by the popular state premier and former federal minister Manuela Schwesig. The 52-year-old heads a coalition with the socialist Left Party. Schwesig stands a good chance of ensuring that this remains the case after the election on September 20.

Schwesig, who for a long time trailed the far-right populist Alternative for Germany party (AfD) by a wide margin in the polls, has been campaigning on the slogan "The woman against blue" — a reference to the AfD's party color.

In a televised debate with AfD lead candidate Leif-Erik Holm just over ten days before the election, the state premier described the AfD as "the most dangerous party for our country, for the economy, for social welfare, and also for us women." Addressing Holm directly, she added: "You are talking the country down."
Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania is not an AfD stronghold
Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania is the only eastern German state where the domestic intelligence agency has not classified the AfD as "confirmed right-wing extremist."

The center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), the party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz, is polling at a historic low, the lowest in any German state. A poor showing in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania could further fuel debate over the increasingly unpopular chancellor. The environmentalist Greens are also fighting to remain in the state parliament, with support hovering around the 5% threshold for representation.

With a vote distribution like this, it is highly unlikely that a majority could be assembled to elect AfD lead candidate Leif-Erik Holm as state premier. After all, every party with a realistic chance of entering the state parliament has ruled out any cooperation with the AfD.

The party's lead candidate, Leif-Erik Holm, deliberately cultivates a down-to-earth image. At campaign events, he draws on his experience as a radio host, including with the public broadcaster NDR. A member of the Bundestag for the Alternative for Germany (AfD) since 2017, he repeatedly taps into widespread dissatisfaction with the government, the economic slowdown, and the comparatively difficult social conditions in the structurally weak and sparsely populated northeast.

Holm cannot match the popular SPD state premier, Schwesig, in head-to-head comparisons of the leading candidates. But the AfD's support in the polls, neck and neck with the SPD, underscores just how deeply divided Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania remains.
Governing the coastal state is unlikely to become any easier in the years to come.
This article has been translated from German.

articles.title: From ovations in Venice to death threats in Israel: the extreme responses to NAZA documentary
articles.summary:
As Gaza documentary wins cinematic acclaim, its directors face vitriol in Israel amid a febrile election campaign

First there was a moment of stunned silence. Then, in the Sala Grande, the…

blocks.text: First there was a moment of stunned silence. Then, in the Sala Grande, the main screening hall of the Venice film festival within the Palazzo del Cinema, the audience stood almost as one and turned to applaud the film-makers for 25 minutes.
The film the audience had watched for 80 harrowing minutes was the Gaza documentary NAZA, which has been produced by the Guardian.
The film’s title comes from an Israeli military acronym used euphemistically to refer to the civilians expected to be killed in a military attack.

Unfolding against the background of Tel Aviv at night, the participants – intelligence officers and other soldiers – describe a series of systems, some powered by AI, that select the thousands who should die in strikes, often at night and surrounded by their families.
Perhaps most challenging for Israel’s political elite is that it is a story told exclusively in Hebrew by 24 anonymised Israeli military insiders, many of them from elite units.

The documentary depicts a wide variety of viewpoints that all lead to the same conclusion: participation in a programme of mass killing where there were few boundaries between combatant and civilian, in a war where more than 73,000 Palestinians have been killed. Some describe being shamed by their experience. Some are neutral. Others describe excitement, and a sense of “fun” as they justify their actions.

It will open in US cinemas from 30 September, with international distribution plans to be announced shortly. The ripples of ovation gathered in volume among the few who have seen the film before its New York premiere, but in Israel the film provoked a very different response.

Rightwing political figures have rushed to accuse its directors – the Oscar-winning Israeli film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor – of “treason”. The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, who has long harboured an antipathy to critical media, declared on Wednesday he would seek new laws to strip citizenship from people who he said “smear” Israeli soldiers.

Demonstrators and members of far-right groups went further still, calling for violence against the pair and the demolition of their homes. Outside Szor’s parents’ house in central Israel, protesters called for the “death penalty for traitors”.

An editorial in the left-leaning newspaper Haaretz warned that their lives were credibly endangered. Dozens of human rights and peace organisations in Israel rallied to defend the film-makers, as did international press freedom organisations.

The whiplash ferocity of the response, even in the midst of a febrile election campaign where Israeli attitudes to the war in Gaza are a central issue, has surprised even those in the Israeli leftwing and human rights community who have long been on the receiving end of such denunciations.

The pushback to the documentary is both a testament to its power and evidence of how the Israeli right is exploiting a film, as yet unseen by most, to craft its own version of what it says it represents.
Critics in Israel seized on the longstanding idea that Israelis should not criticise their country in front of foreign audiences.

Ofer Winter, a controversial former rightwing army officer turned politician, told an election rally for his People of Israel in Rishon LeZion: “An Israeli citizen, a Jew, receives thunderous applause for going out and smearing and defaming his own people.

“I understand that you are afraid to return to Israel,” he taunted the directors. “You are right. You have nothing to return to. It is a disgrace and a shame to return after you spat in the faces of your own people.”

blocks.caption: A protest against the NAZA film-makers in Savyon, Israel. Photograph: Sharon Eilon/Sopa Images/Shutterstock

blocks.text: The rightwing journalist Yehuda Schlesinger of Channel 14, a station regarded as being a mouthpiece for Netanyahu, went further still, saying Abraham and Szor should be “pursued” and “hunted”, prevented from returning to Israel, and describing the ovation in Venice as “25 minutes of antisemitic applause”.
By Wednesday, Netanyahu had decided to weigh in, announcing he would promote two bills to legislate against the “defamation” of Israeli soldiers and the state of Israel.
“We will revoke citizenship for anyone who defames IDF soldiers around the world – he will be deeply hurt in his pocket.”
At points, the threats of violence have been realised.

On Wednesday, the journalist Haggai Matar, a director of the left-leaning independent +972 Magazine and Sicha Mekomit (Local Call), where Abraham’s first reporting on the allegations appeared in collaboration with the Guardian, said their offices had been broken into by rightwing activists who had filmed the intrusion.

“The discussion about NAZA has been a million times more prominent than the UK sanctions announcement,” said Dahlia Scheindlin, an Israeli political and polling expert who writes a column for Haaretz, adding that the right was exploiting the current inability of Israelis to see the film and make their own judgment.
“While it is unseen, it can be turned into something electorally potent that at present Israelis aren’t able to demystify.”

The film has also arrived in the midst of a markedly worsening atmosphere towards dissenting views, acute since Hamas’s deadly attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, with the film challenging a long-held expectation that Israel’s media self-censor in times of conflict.

As Israel has become increasingly isolated internationally over both Gaza, where an independent UN inquiry found Israel continues to commit genocide, and growing settler violence in the occupied West Bank, the film also appears to have touched a more complex nerve in Israel’s collective psyche.
Israel’s forthcoming elections in October have acted as an accelerant for the country’s rightwing parties, whose language has become more hardline and extreme under Netanyahu’s far-right coalition.

Human rights activists, critical journalists, the left more broadly and even the notion of an independent judiciary have long been presented as an enemy within by the far right, who appear to be seeking to weaponise the film against a wider community of critics of Israel and its military.
The extreme response from Netanyahu and his allies has itself been condemned.
The Yedioth Ahronoth columnist Nahum Barnea described the calls to strip the film-makers of their citizenship as “delusional”.

The former editor-in-chief of the Jerusalem Post, Yaakov Katz, wrote: “Not only does such a move not make Israel look stronger, but it creates the impression that we have something to hide and are afraid of criticism. It makes it seem like we fear to stand up for our truth and what we believe in.”
And for Haaretz’s Etan Nechin, who saw the film at a press screening in New York earlier this week, the reaction to NAZA is a symptom of a serious malaise.

“In a healthy democracy, NAZA would be shown on the evening news, its allegations would cause a public outrage and the state would promise a thorough investigation,” he wrote. “Instead, following the film’s Venice premiere, Abraham and Szor have effectively been pushed into exile.”

articles.title: Women's football in Germany booming, but still much to do
articles.summary: Women's football is growing rapidly, particularly in Germany. Nevertheless, equal pay and investment remain major talking points.

image.caption: Women's football in Germany has made strides in recent years, but still has work to do to improve its professional structuresImage: Grant Hubbs/STEINSIEK.CH/IMAGO

blocks.text: According to the German Football Association (DFB), investment in women's football by professional clubs has risen by 135% over the past six years. In addition, the number of girls in Germany who play the game has increased by about 30% since 2022.
Celia Sasic, the former Germany striker who has been in charge of diversity and inclusion at the DFB since 2022, has helped bring women's football more into the spotlight in the boardroom.
"We've focused on the issue and established new structures, so that there is now a separate department with its own sports director," the 38-year-old told DW.
"In my view, it's important that there are very clear responsibilities for the development and professionalization of this sport."

blocks.caption: Celia Sasic has been fighting for equality in women's football for years and wants better structures in the women's game in GermanyImage: Simon Hofmann/Getty Images

blocks.text: "I believe it's important that [women's football] is recognized within the licensed clubs. And it's becoming increasingly recognized, so the framework conditions need to be adjusted," continued Sasic.
"And we're seeing that if we provide the right framework for the game, there's huge growth potential there."
Numbers support growth of women's game

The most-watched football match featuring a German team in 2025 was the Women's European Championship semifinal between Germany and Spain. The match drew around 14.26 million viewers — and a market share of about 57.6%. By comparison, the men's game against Portugal in the Nations League semifinals drew around 10 million viewers.
Sasic, who was part of the German team that won the 2009 and 2013 European championships, regards this as a foundation to build on.
"This is incredibly significant for us as a society and in terms of our influence abroad," she said.
"There are women who play football, who play for us on the national team, and who inspire us so much that millions of us watch their games."
'My biggest role model was Zinedine Zidane'
Sasic is clearly proud of the recent progress. For a long time, women's football in Germany was not taken seriously.
"I had no choice. I had to look to men for role models," Sasic recalled.
"My biggest role model was Zinedine Zidane. I had posters of [Luis] Figo, [David] Beckham, and Michael Ballack hanging in my room."

blocks.caption: Support for the women's team has exploded in recent years in GermanyImage: Eddie Keogh/Getty Images

blocks.text: Posters of women wouldn't have existed back then, but it's different now. These days, Germany captain Giulia Gwinn and players like Jule Brand and Lea Schüller smile down from the walls of children's bedrooms, inspiring girls to dream of a great career in women's football.
Further investment required to push women's game forward

Despite the boom, the financial gap between women's and men's football remains enormous, as figures from the DFB and the German Soccer League (DFL) show. While the 18 Bundesliga clubs spent €1.72 billion ($1.9 billion) on players and coaching staff alone in the 2024–25 season, the personnel expenses of the 12 Women's Bundesliga clubs most recently totaled just under €30 million — about 60 times lower.

Salaries also highlight how the professionalization of women's football is still very much in its infancy. In the 2023-24 season, a women's Bundesliga player earned an average base salary of around €48,000 per year. Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane is estimated to have earned €25 million during the same season.
This disparity is expected to narrow in the future.
"Football reflects our society — and thus also the gender inequality and the gender pay gap that we see in our society," former German Foreign Minister Annalena Baerbock told DW earlier this year.

blocks.caption: Baerbock believes change in terms of equal pay lies in the hands of football nationsImage: Eduardo Munoz/REUTERS

blocks.text: "Unfortunately, this gap in football is even wider in many countries than in other professions. But that is by no means set in stone," added Baerbock, who also served as the president of the United Nations General Assembly from September 2025 to September 2026.

"We know from the USA, the United Kingdom, Norway and Spain that if you really want to invest in women's football, equal pay is an important part of that — especially when it comes to tournament bonuses."
Young women need professional support
Celia Sasic currently sees significant progress when it comes to women's football, although it's still early days in the development process.

"Clubs must provide all the necessary resources to enable this development. Football pitches, medical care, a fitness facility and a coaching staff must be available," said Sasic. "Investing in this ultimately makes the game much better, too."

blocks.caption: Bayern Munich offer some of the best training facilities in the country, but the aim is to improve all the facilities in GermanyImage: Jenni Maul/Eibner-Pressefoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Opportunities for young girls in terms of training also need to improve.
"It's a crucial step to have youth development centers where players are trained — not only athletically, but also professionally. These are essential factors for the success of the women's game."
Education, apprenticeship options must be available

A new DFB rule shows that even basic professional structures still need to be established. Only since the 2025–26 season have teams in the Women's Bundesliga been required to employ assistant coaches, goalkeeper coaches and athletic coaches on a full-time, professional basis.

Sasic and women's football still have a long way to go, but the former player is determined to continue fighting for greater equality. The 2027 Women's World Cup in Brazil is a great place to start, and Sasic is hoping for a successful showing for Germany at the tournament as this would likely give women's football another major boost — and bring broadcasters new record viewership ratings.
This article was originally written in German.
Correction, September 18, 2026: An earlier version of this article misspelled the name of Jule Brand. DW apologizes for the error.

articles.title: Google's Gemini AI hacked three companies in security test
articles.summary: The AI model accessed the internet and guessed credentials to three websites, a Google official told the BBC.

blocks.text: Google's AI model Gemini autonomously hacked into three companies during a test of its cyber-security capabilities, the company has said, in what is thought to be the first known case of it carrying out such an act.
Gemini found "public information online and guessed credentials to access websites it thought were part of the test", a Google official told the BBC, noting that in each instance "the model stopped".
The affected companies have been informed about the breach.

It comes after renewed public scrutiny over the pace of AI development, with some tech firms calling for a slowdown as they raise concerns over its potential threat to humanity - though not all companies agree.
The hacks. first reported by the Wall Street Journal, occurred in May during a test conducted by an independent company that carries out cyber-security evaluations.

Heather Adkins, vice president of Security Engineering at Google, told the BBC in a statement: "We ensured the three entities were made aware, and we worked with our training partner on the changes they've now made to their testing processes."
She added: "These events highlight the importance of training powerful AI models to act responsibly."
Other AI systems have recently reported similar instances of breaches.

In July, Anthropic's Claude escaped its test environment to hack three organisations on its own just days after OpenAI said its models had carried out cyber-attacks against several "publicly available services".
As public debate continues to grow over the safety of developing the tech, so too does conversation around regulation.

Both Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang and OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman are expected to attend a White House state dinner with Chinese President Xi Jinping next Friday. Altman will then brief the UN Security Council next week.
On Friday, Huang told CBS News, the BBC's US partner, "we should go as fast as we can" with AI development.
